Investigations suggest the outbreak may be linked to eggs imported from outside the UK, mainly used in restaurants and cafes.
There is currently no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected by the outbreak.
More than a third of the affected individuals were admitted to hospital, including babies and adults up to the age of 90.
Symptoms of salmonella include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever.

title: Dear Richard: My ungrateful grandson is too lazy to send me photographs from our holiday
author: Richard Madeley
content:
![People walking on a beach](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/family/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498863977_17871540483910_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![People walking on a beach](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/family/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498863977_17871540483910_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dear Richard,
In May I took my beloved 25-year-old grandson on a lavish two-week holiday. He brought a good digital camera and took dozens of photographs, and promised he’d label them and email them to me a couple of weeks after we got back, so I could load them into my digital carousel at home and also show some to friends. After a month I had received neither the pictures nor a word of thanks, so I gently nudged him. Nothing. I then wrote him an email saying I was a little hurt by his radio silence, especially as it had been so lovely to spend some time with him in such beautiful locations. He answered testily, saying he’d been busy – which for all I know he had been – but also that a gift was a gift and should come with no strings attached, and that he didn’t appreciate being “preached” to. As an afterthought he sent a random assortment of perhaps six pictures without the annotations he’d promised.
We have never had a rift before, but I feel very upset at this. Even if the pictures do arrive, I won’t get the pleasure I hoped for from looking at them. I also feel somewhat taken advantage of. Should I speak to his mother (my daughter)?
– P, via TCUK
Dear P,
Of course not. Why drag the lad’s poor mother into your potpourri of injured feelings? What is she supposed to do? Deliver some sort of lecture to her son on explicit gratitude? Prise more photos and snapshots out of him for you? As his mother, she’s more likely to take his side. You’ll just risk making a mildly annoying situation a lot worse. Honestly, P, get a grip.
This is mountains-out-of-molehills territory. You had a great holiday with your grandson. Nothing went wrong. Yes, he was slack about sending you photos afterwards but . . . so what? 25 is the new 15. Young males are maturing much, much later these days. That’s just how it is. But you’re a proper grown-up – so act like one. Kids can be unintentionally rude, callous and ungrateful. It was ever thus. It’s up to us oldies to manage that, and not take it personally.
Come on, P. Your grandson is simply acting his age. I suggest you do the same. Move on.
‘Our son isn’t looking after the bike we got him for his London commutes’
Dear Richard,
Our son recently started working in London and we’ve bought him a bicycle. It’s not super high end but it’s pretty good quality and it means he saves nearly £200 a month on public transport. We are worried that he’s not taking care of it – he leaves it chained up after nights out to retrieve the next day – and it’s only a matter of time before it’s stolen. He says he’s taken out insurance but I suspect they’ll have strict security requirements that he isn’t observing and they’d make a settlement difficult. And then he’d be asking us for a replacement, which we couldn’t easily afford after a spate of other expenses. We’ve shared our concerns but he said there’s no problem and we’re just country mice who think London is some sort of latter-day Sodom and Gomorrah. But we are worried that this is just a replay of the time we got a dog and then ended up looking after it ourselves. How can we induce him to look after his possessions properly?
– G&P, Herts
Dear G&P,
You can’t. None of us can live our grown-up children’s lives for them. We can only offer our best advice and then, frankly, (unless we’re talking matters of life and death) leave them to sink or swim. Sometimes they can only learn by their mistakes.
Your son is clearly being an idiot. If he truly thinks a simple chain and padlock will keep his brand new bike secure (anywhere, let alone crime-cursed London) he needs his head examined. A simple pair of bolt cutters and snap – it’ll be gone. Probably by the time you read this reply.
My advice, if by some miracle that hasn’t happened yet, is to tell him bluntly that when the insurers refuse to cough up the cost of a new bike (which, again, you are absolutely right about; they won’t, they’ll tell him he should have brought it inside overnight) you have no intention of buying him another one. You warned him. He scorned you. He reaps what he sows. It’ll be his reward for what is obviously sheer laziness. He can’t be bothered to secure his bike properly at night. Probably, if I’m being honest, because he didn’t have to pay for it in the first place.
Looking on the bright side, it could prove a valuable life lesson for him when his old commuting costs return to hit him in the pocket again. Facile optimism can come with a price. And parents won’t always be ready and willing to cover that. You certainly shouldn’t.
What a silly boy, though.
summary: An advice columnist responds to two letters from older relatives frustrated by the ungrateful and careless behavior of younger family members. In the first case, a grandmother is upset that her 25-year-old grandson has delayed sending holiday photos and reacted defensively to her gentle nudge. In the second, parents are worried their son will lose or ruin the bicycle they bought him for commuting in London due to poor security habits. The columnist advises both letter writers to let go of their frustrations, avoid involving other family members, and let the young men face natural consequences rather than trying to manage their lives.
key_points: A grandmother took her 25-year-old grandson on a lavish holiday, after which he delayed sending promised photographs and responded testily to her follow-up.
The columnist advised the grandmother against involving her daughter, telling her to stop making a mountain out a molehill and act her age.
Parents bought their son a bicycle for his London commute, but worry he is leaving it insecurely chained overnight and risking theft.
The columnist told the parents they cannot live their adult children's lives and should refuse to buy a replacement if the bike gets stolen.

title: Why does Salmonella cause serious illness in some people but not others?
author: Manal Mohammed
content:
For most people, a Salmonella infection causes gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the stomach and intestines that can mean several miserable days of diarrhoea, cramps, fever or vomiting. Most people recover within a week. But severe diarrhoea and dehydration can still be dangerous, even while the bacteria remain confined to the gut.
In a small minority of patients, however, Salmonella crosses the gut lining and enters the blood. In the current UK outbreak, seemingly caused by eggs imported from abroad, two people have developed bloodstream infections and one death has been associated with the outbreak. How does a familiar cause of food poisoning escape the gut, and why does this only happen to some people?
By August 13 2026, the UK Health Security Agency had identified 207 confirmed cases of a closely related strain of Salmonella Enteritidis. Among patients for whom the relevant information was available, 38% had been admitted to hospital because of their symptoms.
Egg consumption is investigators’ strongest lead, although the source remains unconfirmed. Several affected people ate egg dishes at food businesses supplied by several sources, including importers. Investigators also identified possible opportunities for cross-contamination, in which bacteria are transferred between foods or surfaces, at two premises. They have found no link to UK-produced eggs or poultry.
Salmonella Enteritidis belongs to a broad group called non-typhoidal Salmonella, which is distinct from the bacteria that cause typhoid and paratyphoid fever. Doctors describe an infection as invasive when Salmonella reaches the blood or another part of the body that is normally free of bacteria. A bloodstream infection can lead to sepsis, a life-threatening reaction in which the immune system begins damaging the body’s organs and tissues.
How Salmonella escapes the gut
Genes, which are sections of DNA containing biological instructions, allow Salmonella to build tiny injection systems that work like molecular syringes. One injects proteins into cells lining the gut, causing them to engulf the bacterium. These injection systems are found in many Salmonella bacteria , so their presence cannot explain why one patient develops a bloodstream infection while another has relatively mild diarrhoea. In most people, several layers of immune defence contain the infection in the gut.
A second helps Salmonella alter the membrane-wrapped compartment that forms around it after an immune cell swallows it, allowing some bacteria to survive and multiply. Macrophages are immune cells that engulf and usually destroy microbes. Some Salmonella can survive inside them. This sheltered position is one way the bacteria may move into deeper tissues and the bloodstream, although other routes may contribute.
Why some people become more seriously ill
Scientists have identified more than 2,600 types of Salmonella, known as serovars, although fewer than 100 cause most human illness. A strain is a more closely related genetic branch within one of these types. Both types and strains vary in their tendency to spread.
Nontyphoidal Salmonella that can invade blood are known as invasive serovars and the most predominant serovars associated with blood infections are Typhimurium,Enteritidis, Choleraesuis and Dublin
Records from routine testing in England illustrate the difference. Among more than 116,000 bacterial samples collected between 2004 and 2015, about 2% of Enteritidis samples came from blood, compared with 35% of Salmonella Dublin samples. Testing patterns affect the figures, but the difference indicates that some types spread beyond the gut much more readily than others.
Strains within the same type can also behave differently. Laboratory experiments on two Enteritidis strains, conducted using mouse immune cells, identified genes that help the bacteria survive and multiply inside macrophages. Such experiments identify mechanisms for further study but cannot predict how ill a patient will become.
Age and health also shape the outcome. In the English study, Salmonella was found in blood in 6.5% of samples from adults over 65, compared with 1.9% from adults aged 18 to 64. Newborn babies also had an elevated risk. Weakened immune systems and certain long-term health conditions can make an infection harder to contain.
The number of bacteria swallowed affects the likelihood of becoming ill. Outbreak-based models suggest that heavier contamination increases the risk, although researchers do not know how strongly the amount swallowed affects the likelihood of an infection reaching the blood.
What the current outbreak can tell us
The hospital admission figure deserves attention, but it does not establish that this strain has an unusual ability to cause severe disease. The 38% applies only to patients for whom information was available. Official counts also miss many people whose illness clears before testing, so those with more serious symptoms can be overrepresented. Scientists commenting on the outbreak have urged caution when interpreting the figure.
The UK Health Security Agency used whole-genome sequencing, which involves reading and comparing all or nearly all of the bacteria’s genetic code. Bacteria recovered from patients were very closely related and genetically linked to a 2025 outbreak associated with imported eggs. Sequencing can connect cases and help investigators trace their source. Genetic similarity alone cannot reveal how likely a strain is to cause severe illness.
The Food Standards Agency says pregnant women, babies, young children and older people should eat raw or runny hen eggs only if they carry the British Lion mark or come from the Laid in Britain scheme. These schemes require safety measures including vaccinating hens and additional testing.
Anyone who keeps being sick and cannot retain fluids, has bloody diarrhoea or continues to show signs of dehydration after using rehydration sachets should call NHS 111. The NHS provides further advice on when to seek urgent help.
Investigators will need to combine the bacteria’s genetic code with information about the patients’ health, what and where they ate, and laboratory evidence. Only then can they begin to explain why the infection spread beyond the gut in two patients while most cases caused gastrointestinal illness.
summary: While most Salmonella infections cause temporary gastroenteritis, a small minority of patients develop severe bloodstream infections that can lead to life-threatening complications. In a UK outbreak linked to imported eggs, the UK Health Security Agency identified 207 confirmed cases of Salmonella Enteritidis by August 13, 2026. Illness severity is influenced by factors such as bacterial strain, the number of bacteria swallowed, and the patient's age and immune health.
key_points: By August 13, 2026, the UK Health Security Agency identified 207 confirmed cases of a closely related Salmonella Enteritidis strain in a UK outbreak linked primarily to imported eggs.
While Salmonella typically causes temporary gastroenteritis, it can sometimes cross the gut lining and enter the bloodstream, potentially leading to sepsis.
Certain bacterial strains, higher swallowed doses, older age, newborn status, and weakened immune systems increase the risk of severe illness.
Authorities advise vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, babies, and older adults to only consume raw or runny eggs carrying the British Lion mark or from the Laid in Britain scheme.

title: Infected blood victims told to return compensation
author: Charlotte Gifford
content:
![Demonstrators hold placards reading message related to the NHS infected blood scandal a](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/money/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498847082_17871384169710_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Demonstrators hold placards reading message related to the NHS infected blood scandal a](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/money/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498847082_17871384169710_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Bereaved spouses of infected blood victims have been ordered to return their compensation, The Telegraph can reveal.
In recent weeks, 12 bereaved partners have received letters asking them to return £10,000 payments made up to five years ago.
In a copy of the letter seen by this newspaper, the Government said it had paid the money by mistake: “Unfortunately [...] you were not eligible for the bereavement lump sum and should not have received this payment. We sincerely apologise that this error was not identified at an earlier stage.”
The recipients of the letters had lost spouses and long-term partners to HIV and hepatitis viruses in the infected blood scandal, considered the worst treatment disaster in NHS history. Many are owed large sums in compensation from the Government.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) and the Cabinet Office have suspended the payment requests after several charities and The Telegraph raised the issue. The departments said they were considering “the right and fair outcome” for the group who received the £10,000 in error.
But one widow who received the letter said: “It just feels so callous. To receive this letter out of the blue saying we’re going to deduct £10,000 – it’s so ill-judged and disappointing.”
The Hepatitis C Trust said it was a “horrendous” way to treat victims of the scandal.
Rachel Halford, the charity’s chief executive, said: “If the aim of compensation was to provide peace and resolution to those who’ve suffered, the thought that at any moment they might be contacted to repay part of it flies in the face of that.
“It is unforgivable that people who’ve been through so much now have to live with the fear that the recompense they received for an injustice inflicted on them by the state may be taken away from them, even if the fault for the error lies with the Government.”
More than 30,000 people were infected with HIV and hepatitis viruses between the 1970s and 1990s after being given contaminated blood transfusions and blood-clotting products. More than 3,000 died.
The Government has agreed to pay billions to the victims and their families in an official compensation scheme.
However, some were already receiving financial support through the England Infected Blood Support Scheme, which launched in 2017.
One form of compensation was a £10,000 one-off payment for those whose spouse or partner died before November 2017.
But in 2021, the rules changed so only those whose partners died after November 2017 could receive the payment. The Government said this was to align the scheme with Scotland and Wales.
However, it has since emerged that the Government mistakenly sent the £10,000 payments to 12 individuals whose partners had died before 2017.
![Infected blood victims](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/money/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000378434409_17871380108560_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5yQLQqeH37t50SCyM4-zeGcv5yZLmao6LolmWYJrXns.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Telegraph spoke to one widow who received a letter telling her to repay £10,000. The sender, NHS Business Services Authority, the administrator of an earlier support scheme, suggested reducing her monthly payments from the initial scheme by £1,000 until the sum was recovered.
Sarah, which is not her real name, said: “For me, it’s not about the money – it’s the way they did it. The Government says all these things about treating the infected blood community with empathy and then you get this letter and you think, ‘do you really mean it?’”
She said she became her husband’s carer after he fell ill. “It was a really hard time. I kept working and paying the mortgage. It was only years later the impact hit me.”
The incident also raised questions about the fairness of paying some widows £10,000 and not others. “It appears it was only for recently bereaved spouses and partners – so because I lost him 30 years ago, I don’t qualify for a bereavement payment,” said Sarah.
A government spokesman said: “This issue was brought to the attention of ministers in the DHSC and Cabinet Office in recent days, and they have told officials to suspend any repayment requests while we consider the right and fair outcome for the small group of people who were paid incorrectly in the past.
“Our thoughts remain with all the victims and families who suffered from the appalling injustice of the infected blood scandal, and nobody will want to see those families facing any more hardship or unfairness as a result of failings by the state.”
summary: Bereaved partners of victims from the NHS infected blood scandal were recently sent letters demanding the return of £10,000 bereavement payments that the Government admitted were issued by mistake. Twelve individuals whose partners died before November 2017 received the clawback requests, sparking criticism from charities and recipients who described the action as callous. Following intervention from charities and The Telegraph, the Department of Health and Social Care and the Cabinet Office suspended the payment requests to consider a fair outcome.
key_points: Twelve bereaved spouses of infected blood victims were asked to return £10,000 payments made up to five years ago.
The Government admitted the money was sent by mistake due to a rule change in 2021 regarding the date of bereavement.
Charities and recipients strongly criticized the demands, calling the approach unforgivable and distressing for victims.
The DHSC and the Cabinet Office have suspended the repayment requests while reviewing the situation.

title: Special immune cells in centenarians could be killing cancers before they grow
author: Vishwam Sankaran
content:
Rare cells found in centenarians may be helping preserve their longevity by killing cancers before they grow, a groundbreaking new study reveals.
The specialised immune cells were known to kill some tumour cells. The new study, conducted by researchers at the University of Osaka in Japan, shows that they also play a role in healthy ageing among centenarians.
The cells are called CD4 CTL and are a signature of supercentenarians who live past 110, researchers say.
“CD4 CTLs are an atypical and relatively rare T cell population,” Kosuke Hashimoto, author of the new study published in the journal Cell Reports, said. “So, their marked increase in supercentenarians may provide important clues as to how the immune system is maintained in extreme old age.”
The cells clone themselves when the immune system is under attack – a process known as clonal expansion – indicating that they enable older adults to respond to persistent threats.
In the study, researchers analysed blood samples of 28 adults divided into three age groups – 70–99, 100–109, and 110 and older – and found that the proportion of CD4 CTLs among a person’s immune cells seemed to grow with age.
“The selective expansion of certain T cells suggests that, even in extreme old age, the immune system may continue to adapt to age-related challenges,” Dr Hashimoto said.
CD4 CTL expansion seems to begin around the age of 100, researchers say, but it may not always be unique to centenarians and supercentenarians. In fact, it was a participant under the age of 100 who had the highest proportion of these cells.
![CD4 CTL immune cells are a signature of supercentenarians](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/3/05/An-old-woman-holds-a-cane-in-her-hand.jpeg)
In one centenarian’s blood sample, researchers found a single clone of CD4 CTLs accounted for over 50 per cent of their CD4 CTLs.
Scientists then compared the structure of molecules on the surface of each participant’s top CD4 CTL clone with molecules in a public database. Almost three dozen of the matches belonged to people with lung, breast, and liver cancers, the study found.
Since none of the centenarians or supercentenarians had been diagnosed with any of these cancers, their CD4 CTL expansion likely reflected early immune responses against the development of cancer.
“Some CD4 CTLs may recognise cancer-related targets, although their exact targets remain unknown,” Dr Hashimoto said.
The study, however, does not prove that an abundance of CD4 CTLs in the body prevents cancer or causes a person to live longer.
“As we age, abnormal cells, including senescent and cancerous cells, become more common,” Dr Hashimoto said.
“Our findings suggest that immune adaptation to these changes may contribute to exceptional longevity.”
summary: A new study by researchers at the University of Osaka reveals that rare immune cells called CD4 CTLs are found in high proportions in centenarians and supercentenarians. These cells clone themselves in response to persistent threats and showed molecular matches with targets related to lung, breast, and liver cancers. Researchers suggest that the expansion of these specialized immune cells may reflect early responses against cancer development, potentially contributing to exceptional longevity.
key_points: Specialized immune cells known as CD4 CTLs are found in high proportions in centenarians and supercentenarians.
These cells undergo clonal expansion, allowing the immune system to adapt to age-related challenges and persistent threats.
Analysis of top CD4 CTL clones revealed matches with molecules associated with lung, breast, and liver cancers.
The presence of these cells in healthy centenarians suggests they may help kill cancers before they grow, though direct causation is not proven.

title: Salmonella in eggs? I groaned. Not again
author: Edwina Currie
content:
![Hand Pick chicken egg from egg carton box into refrigerator](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498855457_17871577714410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLFvFcbCCSSPOPEZoCZQZEmScts_MJCIICfhGZ0ARPWw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Hand Pick chicken egg from egg carton box into refrigerator](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498855457_17871577714410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLFvFcbCCSSPOPEZoCZQZEmScts_MJCIICfhGZ0ARPWw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
When the news came that one person had died and over 200 people had been taken ill due to salmonella in eggs, I groaned. Not again. It’s a notifiable disease these days, so there’s none of the argument that occurred back in 1988 when thousands were taken ill, around 60 died and yet the witless Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food claimed it was all the fault of housewives being careless with kitchen hygiene.
The resulting furore changed my career, but it also turbocharged attitudes to food safety and legislation. We happily eat around 40 million eggs a day now without fear. So British egg producers must have sighed with relief on hearing that the likely culprits weren’t British; they were imported.
It turns out we import around one in eight of our eggs and rising, perhaps another example of the casual destruction of British farming and food production as government ministers shrug with indifference. So should we ban these imports? It looks like an obvious move to some. Maybe President Trump has a point when he wants to curb imports to encourage domestic production; perhaps we should try something similar.
“I’m an economist, not a biologist,” I said to British egg producers when they approached me in the 1990s to help them out of the mess I’d highlighted so effectively. “When you can tell me not one UK-produced egg is contaminated, I will tell everyone.” And they did, investing monumental effort, science and capital into that process, and succeeded in 2004. Ever since, our industry can be very proud of standards which they fiercely protect.
So what do the economics of these imports look like? It’s a rapidly changing picture. Until recently (2022) imported eggs came mainly from the Netherlands, but now it’s Poland, Spain and Ukraine. In fact Ukraine is currently the leading country. Why? It has to be because they’re cheaper, and that’s partly because they still use battery cages, while ours are mostly free range. Traditional barren battery cages were banned in the UK, indeed throughout the EU, in 2012 – although “enriched” cages live on at home too.
![Close up of young Asian woman grocery shopping in a supermarket](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498867759_17871577282281_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In April this year, the British Egg Industry Council (BEIC) in its report Shell Shocked fretted about poorer foreign standards and talked about “dumping”. According to the report, imported egg volumes have increased by around 60 per cent since 2021, climbing from one billion to 1.6 billion eggs annually. Ukraine in particular has become the major supplier following tariff-free access agreed in 2022 and extended to 2028. And we’re talking many millions of pounds here.
So a ban would be a huge blow to a country at war, right away. It’d hit Poland, which is geared up to fend off the Russians too. It’d hit our friends where it hurt, badly, and would land a heavy blow against free trade, which (unlike Trump) I’m old-fashioned enough to believe benefits both sides of the transaction. It’d immediately push up prices over here, affecting consumers, caterers and manufacturers alike; with inflation creeping up again, that’s probably a no-no. A blanket ban would also hurt many excellent foreign producers and could create a backlash – deterring their citizens from buying British. It is so not a good idea!
Fortunately the BEIC has a better suggestion. They say imported eggs and egg products should be required to meet the same standards as those produced under the British Lion Code. Their report also calls for stronger border inspections, improved labelling transparency, and greater support for domestic producers.
I’m not sure about the “government support” bit; lower taxes for everyone would be preferable. But I’d add that we should send teams into Ukraine to discuss with their agriculture ministry how to achieve our high standards, the rigour and vigilance that has led to such success here. Could we encourage some large UK egg producers to open facilities near Lviv or Odesa, to show the locals how it’s done? Could we share and assist with testing regimes in government laboratories? Spreading sound science never hurt anybody; it might grow trade in animal vaccines, to the benefit of our pharmaceutical industry. This could be important commercial business for Ukraine, after the war is over.
We ban too much, in my view, often with unwanted consequences. Just check that your eggs have the British Lion and an 8-digit origin stamp on them; that means they’re from tested hens and farms. Eggy soldiers, anyone?
Edwina Currie served as Junior Health Minister from 1986-1988
summary: Recent salmonella cases linked to imported eggs have raised food safety concerns and highlighted a rise in foreign egg imports. While some might advocate for a ban on these imports, doing so could harm allied nations like Ukraine and Poland and increase domestic food prices. Instead, industry groups and experts suggest enforcing matching safety standards, improving border inspections and labelling, and sharing high production standards with foreign producers.
key_points: One person died and over 200 people fell ill due to salmonella in eggs, with the source traced to imported rather than British eggs.
The UK now imports about one in eight of its eggs, with countries like Ukraine, Poland, and Spain serving as major suppliers.
Imported eggs have increased by around 60 percent since 2021, driven partly by lower costs and practices such as battery cages.
A blanket ban on imported eggs is discouraged because it could harm allied countries, damage free trade, and raise consumer prices.
Proposed solutions include requiring imported eggs to meet British Lion Code standards, improving border checks, and assisting foreign producers with testing.

title: I’m constantly lectured by my holier-than-thou 11-year-old
author: Catherine Balavage; Charlotte Lytton
content:
![Catherine Balavage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000498638262_17869735637710_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbWJXtw86-68av9QfHOuDsm5k5Nh2f7B7beZ9IJPcxR8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Catherine Balavage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000498638262_17869735637710_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbWJXtw86-68av9QfHOuDsm5k5Nh2f7B7beZ9IJPcxR8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Angela Rayner admitted last week that her children are “disgusted” by her vaping habit – something she does so often, they call her the “vape dragon”. My 11-year-old is yet to come up with a nickname for me based on my bad habits, but when it comes to my drinking or eating nachos, he has made his feelings known.
We were on holiday last month when my husband and I got a starter of nachos ahead of our meal. We don’t eat like this every day, but had told our son that he can eat whatever he wants on holiday – it’s a free pass. Instead of being delighted, as I assumed most children of his age would be, he said: “It’s not healthy. Are you sure you should be eating that at your age?” I ate the nachos anyway, but perhaps I enjoyed them a little less after that conversation.
The same goes for alcohol. I probably only drink around once a fortnight, except for special occasions, like being on holiday. But anytime I do, he’ll say: “My teaching assistant told me alcohol is poison – you shouldn’t be drinking, Mum. Is it good for you?” He’s not saying it in a mean way, but he’ll reiterate the advice he’s apparently getting from other grown-ups in his orbit, telling me that wine is “not a health drink”.
He then gave me a list of all the adults he knew who don’t drink, delighted to tell me that they were teetotal, which is a word I doubt I knew at his age.
![Angela Rayner](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/14/TELEMMGLPICT000352626444_17867230353310_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqD3d2dmOlWYuQkR76XZjLQKOylOV7i1cNNz18XOj47vE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
When he first brought the issue up, he clearly already had a bee in his bonnet about it. But it’s very easy to be moral and judgemental when you’re 11. You’ve got a clean slate and your entire life in front of you, and you haven’t yet picked up any vices because you’ve never had the stress to need to. At that age, you’re coming into yourself and becoming a teenager, while developing all sorts of opinions along the way. For parents, there is often the added problem when their children do have a point.
Rayner took up vaping to replace smoking, something that, when she was growing up, was considered “cool”. That also applies to alcohol. I’m 41, and when I was young, if you didn’t drink, people thought you were weird, and you were essentially socially excluded. Someone not drinking would always be brought up – it was considered that strange. There was a lot of peer pressure to drink, even if you didn’t want to. Gen Z seems to have steered away from that, but for my son, who is Generation Alpha, that aversion is even stronger.
It’s not only alcohol that they’re opposed to (and nachos). I thought that at 11, my son and his friends would be far too young to be talking about things like being body conscious, but I was completely wrong. He’s already mentioned abs and wanting to go to the gym. They’re all obsessed with being healthy.
If I offer my son snacks before dinner, he’ll refuse them because he doesn’t want to fill up before his meal. If I give him a bag of sweets, he’ll only eat a few because “he doesn’t want to get sick”, and leaves the rest for later. When he sees me drinking fizzy drinks, he’ll tell me to drink water. His generation is very concerned with being hydrated, which I definitely don’t remember 30 years ago.
Growing up, my parents smoked – which I hated – so I do get where Rayner’s children are coming from. However, I’ve definitely tried to model healthy habits for my four children, aged eight months to 11, so I would like to think we lead by a decent example. I’m an author working from home, which means I can home-cook most meals, and they eat a lot of vegetables and do plenty of exercise.
In many ways, my diet is worse than theirs. It’s that classic conundrum of spending all of your time preparing something healthy for them, and then being so exhausted by the end of it that you just eat leftovers and biscuits for your dinner instead. Thankfully, my son’s ultra-healthiness hasn’t seemed to have affected his siblings yet. My eight-year-old is obsessed with chocolate, while my five-year-old loves fruit.
![Catherine Balavage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000498638322_17869736834460_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Children love to give you their opinions – they’re cheeky like that. But when I do get scolded about my habits, I tell my son: “Everything in moderation, including moderation.”
The “clean eating” phase a while back, which advocated unprocessed food, is definitely not something that I want him to be thinking about. Food isn’t “dirty” – food is food. You can have nachos if you want, or a burger – just go for a walk afterwards. You can eat most things as long as you’re balancing it out with other healthy activities. I want him to understand that instead of seeing things as completely off-limits. It’s better not to get hung up on the small stuff. I also want him to have a good view of life and the world, and not think he has to be healthy all the time.
Having said that, it’s hard to imagine him drinking alcohol, mostly because he’s my baby. I can’t conceive of that at this point, but when he’s grown up, having the occasional beer or glass of wine sometimes wouldn’t bother me. Whether his current attitude towards alcohol changes as he gets older is another question.
I think part of what can drive this puritanical stage for children is that they start realising that their parents might not be around forever, and that scares them. So anything that might speed up that process – like drinking – makes them worried. Someone has obviously told him that alcohol is poison, and he’s thinking: “I don’t want this for my parents.”
While it does sometimes feel like he’s telling me off, I try and remind myself that it’s probably coming from a place of fear and insecurity about us one day not being here. Ultimately, it’s just his attempt at trying to keep us around.
As told to Charlotte Lytton.
summary: The author shares her experience of being constantly lectured by her 11-year-old son about her diet, alcohol consumption, and overall health choices. While the child's puritanical and health-conscious attitude reflects wider generational shifts away from vices, the author believes his scolding ultimately stems from a place of fear and insecurity about his parents' mortality.
key_points: The author's 11-year-old son frequently criticizes her for eating nachos and consuming alcohol, repeating advice he received from school and other adults.
Children belonging to Generation Alpha show a significantly stronger aversion to alcohol and unhealthy habits compared to previous generations.
The 11-year-old and his peers are already hyper-focused on health, hydration, and physical fitness, such as wanting gym access and worrying about body consciousness.
The author believes her son's lecturing behavior is an unconscious attempt to keep his parents healthy and around for a long time out of fear of losing them.

title: People Who Live Past 100 Have a Surprising Abundance of Cancer-Killing Immune Cells
author: Jess Cockerill
content:
Today, the average human lives for about 71 years.
A rare few people will see their 100th birthday, earning the title of centenarian, and even fewer will live past 110.
We call these folks supercentenarians.
New research published in Cell Press reveals one possible explanation for how these superagers might be dodging the mounting risk of cancer and illness as the years progress.
At around 100 years, a rare form of T helper cells seems to proliferate in these lucky people, expanding and adapting as time marches on.
"These cells exhibit stepwise differentiation and cytokine plasticity, suggesting adaptive responses to persistent antigens during healthy aging," the study's authors write.
![Rare Cancer-Killing Immune Cells Could Be Protecting People Who Live Beyond 110](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-19-at-13.41.45-675x675.png)
We all have T helper cells (aka CD4 cells) as part of our adaptive immune system.
There are many different kinds of CD4 cells, some rarer than others. Cytotoxic CD4 T cells (CD4 CTLs), for instance, are usually quite infrequent in the human body.
These T cells are killers rather than helpers: their job is to patrol the body looking for infected, damaged, or cancerous cells to destroy before further damage is done.
However, as people age into their 90s and beyond, these usually rare CD4 CTLs seem to become increasingly prolific.
This statistically significant pattern appeared in blood samples from a group of 28 Japanese participants (which, admittedly, is a very small sample size, and with citizens of just one country, not necessarily representative of the global human population).
In the samples from eight people in their 70s, 80s, and 90s, the median proportion of CD4 CTLs was 4 percent.
Among the 10 centenarians in the study, the median was 9.6 percent – and in supercentenarians, it was 17.6 percent.
But even in this small sample, there were outliers: one participant who had yet to turn 100 actually had the highest proportion of these cells in their blood.
These cells were active, showing no signs of exhaustion.
"Immune aging is not simply a process of decline," says immunologist Kosuke Hashimoto, of the University of Osaka in Japan.
"The selective expansion of certain T cells suggests that, even in extreme old age, the immune system may continue to adapt to age-related challenges."
By examining proteins on the surface of the cells, the researchers found that these CD4 CTLs emerged when helper cells lost the protein CD27, and then CD28.
Killer T cells are known to clone themselves in response to an immune attack, to form a microscopic army.
This is exactly what the researchers saw in the older adults' blood samples.
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
On average, around 33 percent of the CD4 CTLs in their blood were clones of just one original cell.
In a sample from one centenarian, about half of their CD4 CTLs were copies of the same cell.
This suggests that past a certain age, the human body is faced with increasing immune threats. An abundance of CD4 CTLs could be helping supercentenarians (at least, those living in Japan) survive them.
Related: The Blood of Centenarians Reveals 37 Proteins Linked With Slower Aging
"As we age, abnormal cells, including senescent and cancerous cells, become more common," Hashimoto says.
"Our findings suggest that immune adaptation to these changes may contribute to exceptional longevity."
The research was published in Cell Press.
summary: New research published in Cell Press reveals that centenarians and supercentenarians have a surprisingly high abundance of cytotoxic CD4 T cells, which are cancer-killing immune cells. Blood samples from Japanese participants showed that the proportion of these cells increased with age, reaching a median of 17.6 percent in supercentenarians. These active, cloning cells suggest that the human immune system continues to adapt to age-related challenges in extreme old age.
key_points: Centenarians and supercentenarians exhibit a proliferation of cytotoxic CD4 T cells (CD4 CTLs), which patrol the body to destroy infected, damaged, or cancerous cells.
A study of 28 Japanese participants found that the median proportion of these cells was 4 percent in people in their 70s to 90s, 9.6 percent in centenarians, and 17.6 percent in supercentenarians.
These specialized killer T cells showed high levels of clonal expansion and active states without signs of exhaustion.
The findings indicate that immune aging is not merely a decline, but can involve adaptive responses that help protect against cancer and illness in extreme longevity.

title: Alex Ungar obituary
author: Simon Ungar; Guardian staff reporter
content:
My father, Alex Ungar, who has died aged 91, was a senior lecturer in pharmacology at Edinburgh University for more than 20 years, and a former editor of the British Journal of Pharmacology.
Born in Prague, to Malvina (nee Bojko), a paediatrician, and Josef Ungar, a doctor and research microbiologist, Alex was a happy child until, aged four, his world turned upside down when Germany invaded Czechoslovakia; he never forgot the sight of the tanks rolling through the streets. Two weeks later, his family travelled to London as refugees on a Quaker transport by train via Germany and the Netherlands.
After being temporarily housed in a Quaker community in the village of Jordans, Buckinghamshire, they settled in Pinner, north-west London, where Alex attended Little St John’s prep (now St John’s prep) and Merchant Taylors’ school in Northwood. As a teenager he embarked on lifelong passions for sailing and horse-riding.
He studied medicine at St John’s College, Oxford, and completed his medical training at University College hospital in London in 1962. That year he married Rosalind Stanford, later a teacher, whom he had known since childhood through their shared love of horse-riding, and they settled in Islington, north London.
Alex taught physiology at St Bartholomew’s hospital, then developed his interest in pharmacology at the school of pharmacy (now part of University College London), before moving to Edinburgh in 1969 to take up a lectureship, specialising in cardiac pharmacology. Passionate about his work, he supervised a string of PhD students, and also ran the pharmacology honours programme, which combined medical and science undergraduate students.
He published more than 60 journal articles during his career, collaborating with colleagues worldwide. At the British Journal of Pharmacology from 1973 to 1984, he supported many younger colleagues in publishing their research. Resolutely anti-hierarchical, he led by example and was an inspiration for many.
From 1962 to 2014, Alex was also the chief medical adviser to the pharmaceutical company Norgine. He was elected as an honorary fellow of the British Pharmacological Society in 2006.
Alex’s intellect was prodigious and his thirst for knowledge and skills insatiable and wide-ranging. His conversation was scintillating, peppered with witty anecdotes. He read widely, in philosophy, history and literature, while maintaining a penchant for classic thrillers. He was a polyglot and a passionate European, who recently delighted in regaining his Czech citizenship. A wine connoisseur, he was wine-buyer for Edinburgh University’s staff club for many years. Friends and family also benefited from his superb culinary skills, ranging from full-blown cordon bleu menus to the perfect omelette.
After Alex retired from Edinburgh in 1991, he and Rosalind moved to Cumbria, where they continued to walk with their dogs, sail, travel and attend concerts and especially operas.
Alex is survived by Rosalind, their three children, Jonah, Pippa and me, three grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.
summary: Alex Ungar, a senior lecturer in pharmacology at Edinburgh University and former editor of the British Journal of Pharmacology, has died at the age of 91. Born in Prague, he and his family fled to London as refugees following the 1939 German invasion of Czechoslovakia. He pursued a distinguished medical and academic career, publishing over 60 journal articles and serving as chief medical adviser to Norgine. A man of wide-ranging intellect and diverse personal passions, he retired to Cumbria in 1991 and is survived by his wife, Rosalind, three children, three grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.
key_points: Alex Ungar was born in Prague and arrived in London as a refugee at the age of four following the German invasion of Czechoslovakia.
He studied medicine at St John's College, Oxford, completing his training at University College Hospital in 1962.
He worked as a senior lecturer in cardiac pharmacology at Edinburgh University from 1969 until his retirement in 1991.
He served as editor of the British Journal of Pharmacology from 1973 to 1984 and was chief medical adviser to Norgine from 1962 to 2014.
He was made an honorary fellow of the British Pharmacological Society in 2006.

title: Sugary drinks found linked to stomach cancer for first time
author: Vishwam Sankaran
content:
People who drink sugary beverages daily are at a higher risk of developing stomach cancer, a new study warns while hinting that artificial sweeteners can lower the danger.
Previous research has widely linked sugar-sweetened beverages with an increased risk of colorectal, breast, and liver cancers, but evidence on gastric cancer has been limited.
The new study found that people who consumed at least one serving of a sugar-sweetened beverage a day carried twice the risk of gastric cancer compared with those who consumed less than a serving per month.
“This is the first study to demonstrate an association between sugar-sweetened beverage intake and gastric cancer in a US population,” Andrew Chan, author of the study published in the journal Gastro Hep Advances, said.
“Gastric cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer death worldwide, but we’ve known very little about how diet might contribute to this cancer.”
![Soda sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/3/03/Soda-sweetened-with-high-fructose-corn-syrup.jpeg)
The study assessed the health and lifestyle data from 112,000 people spanning several decades and found that 278 of them developed gastric cancer. The link was observed in both women and men.
Fructose was the main sweetener in the drinks consumed by the participants, which was found to be associated with greater gastric cancer incidence.
In women, daily consumption of more than one sugar-sweetened beverage – punch, lemonade, sports drinks – was associated with an almost three-fold higher risk of gastric cancer, compared to those who did so rarely.
In comparison, the study found that higher consumption of artificially sweetened and low-calorie carbonated beverages wasn’t associated with a higher incidence of gastric cancer.
![Apple juice contains high content of vitamin C](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/3/48/Of-the-17-samples-analyzed-the-one-with-the-highest-vitamin-C-content-was-apple-juice.jpeg)
Previous research has shown that infection by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of gastric cancer. The latest study assessed the H pylori status in a subset of 940 participants, and found that there was no association between sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and infection by this bacterium.
Citing the main limitation of the study, researchers said the findings were observational and didn’t establish a causal link.
There was also limited information from participants on their H pylori status and family history of gastric cancer.
The study participants were predominantly white, constraining the ability of researchers to examine differences across racial and ethnic groups.
However, since the analysed data included lifestyle information gathered over many years, researchers said they could control for many potential risk factors for gastric cancer. They called for further studies to confirm the findings and investigate why sugar-sweetened beverages increased the danger of gastric cancer.
summary: A new study of 112,000 people links daily consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages to an increased risk of gastric cancer in a US population for the first time. The findings showed that consuming at least one sugary drink a day doubled the risk of stomach cancer, with women experiencing a nearly three-fold higher risk. Conversely, the research found no association between artificially sweetened drinks and a higher incidence of gastric cancer.
key_points: Consuming at least one sugary drink daily was linked to twice the risk of gastric cancer compared to consuming less than one serving per month.
Fructose was the primary sweetener associated with greater gastric cancer incidence among participants.
Daily consumption of sugary beverages in women was associated with an almost three-fold higher risk of gastric cancer.
Higher consumption of artificially sweetened and low-calorie beverages showed no association with a higher incidence of gastric cancer.
Researchers noted that the findings were observational and did not establish a causal link.

title: Labour under pressure to restore men’s right to prostate cancer tests
author: Michael Searles
content:
Labour is under pressure to reinstate middle-aged men’s right to tests that help detect prostate cancer.
Last week, The Telegraph revealed that men aged over 50 were no longer entitled to a blood test to help identify the disease, with GPs instead deciding who is given one.
Previously, any man over the age of 50 had been entitled to a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test via their GP, even if they did not have symptoms.
The Government is now facing increasing pressure to reverse its decision to remove that right, including calls from the Conservative Party.
Stuart Andrew MP, the shadow health secretary, said it “looks like a further restriction of patient choice with a service that was on offer now disappearing”.
“PSA tests are a credible aid for the early identification of prostate cancer. Labour’s restrictions risk leaving men without answers,” he told The Telegraph.
“Requiring information on genetic heritage and family history is particularly concerning when many people simply do not have accurate family medical records. No man with potential prostate cancer symptoms should be denied a test because of poor family records.”
He said the Conservatives would “back the latest evidence and research to ensure patient care remains at the heart of testing guidance”.
summary: The Labour government is facing pressure from the Conservative Party and other critics to reverse a decision that removes the right of men over 50 to receive a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test without symptoms. Previously, any man in this age group could request the test via their GP, but access is now determined by GPs using criteria that include family history and genetic heritage. Critics argue this restriction risks leaving men without answers and limits patient choice in early cancer detection.
key_points: Men over 50 are no longer automatically entitled to a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test via their GP if they are asymptomatic.
GPs now decide which patients receive the screening test based on factors such as family history and genetic heritage.
The Labour government faces growing pressure, including from the Conservative Party, to reverse the policy change.
Critics argue that relying on family medical history is concerning because many individuals lack accurate records.

title: Active Surveillance Rises as Focal Therapy Persists
author: Frederik Joelving
content:
Rates of surveillance have continued to grow among US veterans with low-risk or favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer, in line with guidelines, while thousands of patients nationally continue to receive focal therapy despite limited evidence supporting its use, according to a pair of new papers.
In one study, data from the Veterans Affairs Healthcare System showed that between 2005 and 2024, active surveillance/watchful waiting rose from 27% to 93% in men with low-risk disease, and from 14% to 61% in those with favorable intermediate-risk disease.
The other study, using data from the National Cancer Database, found that more than 15,000 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2023 — or 1.3% of the study population — received focal therapy such as laser ablation or high-intensity focused ultrasound. However, such treatment remains investigational and is not backed by high-quality evidence.
The two studies were published online on August 13 in JAMA, alongside an accompanying editorial.
The studies “show real progress, in that surveillance is finally treated as disciplined care rather than therapeutic inaction,” Spyridon P. Basourakos, MD, of Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, and colleagues wrote in the editorial, titled “The Emperor’s New Clothes — The Discipline of Evidence.”
The studies “also expose a growing concern, in that focal therapy is presented as elegant and individualized when it usually amounts to overtreatment or undertreatment, with no quality data to demonstrate that it is superior to other noninvasive standard of care options,” wrote Basourakos, along with coauthors Jonathan E. Shoag, MD, and Daniel E. Spratt, MD.
The increase in active surveillance is “gratifying,” said David Einstein, MD, a prostate cancer specialist at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, who was not involved in the research.
While the paper on focal therapies “raises troubling questions,” he added, the analysis “didn’t necessarily exclude cases” in which the treatment was used to “address obstructive urinary symptoms before proceeding to traditional radiation.” Considering this point and the low overall use, “I don’t necessarily think this article points to a massive problem,” Einstein said.
A Look at the Data
According to current guidelines, active surveillance is the preferred management approach for low-risk and many intermediate-risk prostate cancers, while focal therapy is recommended only for intermediate-risk disease in clinical trials or prospective registries. For low-risk disease, focal therapy may represent overtreatment, whereas for high- and very-high-risk disease, there is insufficient high-level evidence.
To characterize recent management trends, the VA study assessed use of active surveillance/watchful waiting between 2005 and 2024 in men with favorable-risk prostate cancer.
Grace Lee, MD, of the San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, and colleagues classified patients as being on active surveillance or watchful waiting if they did not receive treatment within 15 months of their diagnostic biopsy and had one or more prostate-specific antigen (PSA) values ≥ 1 ng/mL during this time, or if they received a confirmatory biopsy within 3-15 months after their diagnostic biopsy and before any active treatment.
The median age of the more than 73,000 men in the study was 65 years. As the use of surveillance as initial management rose over time, rates of radiation and surgery dropped from more than 40% and 20%, respectively, to single digits in men with low-risk disease and to just below 20% in those with favorable intermediate-risk disease.
On subgroup analysis, surveillance rates for patients with PSA levels < 10 ng/mL and Gleason grade group 2 in less than 50% of cores rose from 11% to 55%. The rates increased from 27% to 88% for men with Gleason grade group 1 and PSA level 10-20 ng/mL.
Multivariable logistic regression showed increasing age and more recent diagnosis were tied to higher odds of surveillance. By contrast, people who were Black (odds ratio [OR], 0.95 vs White; P < .001) or Hispanic (OR, 0.85 vs non-Hispanic; P = .003) or lived in more disadvantaged neighborhoods had lower odds of receiving active surveillance — a trend that “might be exacerbated outside of a VA system,” said Einstein, “so there is still room for improvement.”
The other study, by Andrea Cosenza, MD, of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, and colleagues, analyzed data from the National Cancer Database.
The researchers classified focal therapy as inappropriate in low-, high-, or very-high-risk disease, and reported intermediate-risk disease separately as the database “does not capture trial enrollment, registry participation, or lesion characteristics needed to classify appropriateness,” they wrote.
Among a study population of nearly 1.18 million men 50 and older, 15,672 received focal therapy. Fifty-one percent had low-, high-, or very-high-risk disease, and 49.0% had intermediate-risk disease.
More intermediate-risk patients received focal therapies in 2023 than in 2010 (2.9% vs 2.1%, P < .001), while the proportion dropped in men with unfavorable intermediate-risk (1.9% vs 2.5%), high-risk (0.9% vs 2.1%), and very-high-risk disease (0.5% vs 1.8%). Additionally, there was no significant change in the proportion of patients with low-risk disease who received focal therapies between 2010 (1.8%) and 2023 (2.2%).
The use of cryotherapy fell, whereas laser ablation and other tumor-destruction methods such as high-intensity focused ultrasound became more popular during the study period.
Focal therapy techniques, including newer ones, “deserve evaluation on their own evidence. Yet as the number of devices has grown, the evidence has not,” the editorialists wrote.
“The patterns of adoption deepen the concern,” Basourakos, Shoag, and Spratt added. The study found that, compared with radical prostatectomy, focal therapy was more common among older and sicker patients, at community programs, and at higher-volume centers.
Although the use seems limited overall, “we should certainly be cautious about overselling patients on an emerging technology,” Einstein agreed.
“I do have concerns that these focal approaches may risk messier salvage treatments in those patients at higher risk who subsequently recur and may risk over treatment in patients who should really be encouraged to pursue active surveillance,” he added.
Funding information is not available in the papers. Several study authors reported disclosures in their publications (a full list can be viewed here and here). Einstein reported receiving honoraria from several drugmakers.
summary: Two new studies published in JAMA show that active surveillance rates for US veterans with low-risk and favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer increased substantially between 2005 and 2024, aligning with clinical guidelines. However, national data also reveal that thousands of patients continue to receive focal therapy despite limited high-quality evidence supporting its use and potential risks of over- or undertreatment. Editorialists and experts note that while the rise in surveillance represents positive progress, the ongoing use of investigational focal therapies warrants caution.
key_points: Active surveillance or watchful waiting among US veterans rose from 27% to 93% for low-risk prostate cancer and from 14% to 61% for favorable intermediate-risk disease between 2005 and 2024.

Data from the National Cancer Database showed that more than 15,000 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2023 received focal therapy, which remains largely investigational and lacks robust supporting evidence.
Racial and ethnic disparities were noted in the VA study, with Black and Hispanic patients showing lower odds of receiving active surveillance.
Editorialists raised concerns that focal therapy is often presented as individualized care but risks resulting in overtreatment, undertreatment, or complicated salvage therapies.

title: Scientists Discover a New Organ Hiding in The Skull
author: Michael Irving
content:
After centuries of medical science, it's reasonable to assume that we have a complete tally of all the organs in the human body by now.
But scientists just keep discovering new ones working thanklessly in the background, performing vital functions like sensing pain or producing saliva.
The latest is all in your head. In a new study published in Nature, biologists at Washington University (WashU) School of Medicine in St. Louis have identified a new immune organ inside the skull.
From that crucial post, it seems to act like a 'security station' to fight brain cancer at the early stages.
So far this organ has only been found in mice, but the researchers say there are signs that humans have them, too. And if we can supercharge these structures, we might have a new weapon against deadly brain cancers.
"This study reveals that the skull bone marrow is far more than just a structural framework – it harbors previously unrecognized hubs for brain-specific immune responses," says Jonathan Kipnis, a brain immunologist at WashU and senior author of the new study.
"Uncovering this localized immune niche changes how we view neuroimmune interactions and opens exciting new avenues for treating brain tumors and other neurological diseases."
![Scientists Discover a New Organ Hiding in The Skull](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/brain-lymphoids-2.png)
The human body is patrolled by not one, but two distinct immune systems – one for the central nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord, and one for the rest of the body.
It's long been thought that the two systems were completely separate, and in fact, immune cells from the peripheral system can cause all sorts of trouble if they get into the brain. Some are known to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases because the sensitive tissues in the nervous system can be harmed by the 'reckless' techniques that work elsewhere in the body.
But a growing body of research suggests there's a bit more crossover than previously thought. In previous work, the team behind the new study identified tiny channels running from brain tissue, through the dura mater (the outermost protective membrane around the brain) and into the skull itself.
This time, the researchers used fluorescent tracer proteins to observe how molecules moved along these channels, following them from neurons into the bone marrow of the skull.
Eventually they tracked them into what looked suspiciously like germinal centers – structures that form in lymph nodes and act like training camps for immune cells.
Basically, naive B cells enter these structures, multiply to great numbers, get armed, are handed 'Wanted' posters for particular pathogens by other immune cells, and are sent out into battle.
![Scientists Discover a New Organ Hiding in The Skull](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/Germinal-center.jpeg)
In this case, these training camps are strategically located near the brain, so they can fight on the front lines without having to recruit soldiers from further afield in the body.
"We have never seen such structures in healthy bone marrow before," says Jang Hyun Park, cell biologist at WashU and first author of the study.
"It is an exciting discovery that points out that a complex brain requires its own specialized immune structures to defend it."
The researchers tested that idea in mouse models of glioma, a particularly nasty form of brain cancer. They altered the activity of these lymphoid structures by applying a hydrogel laced with either immune-promoting or immune-suppressing compounds under the scalp.
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
Mice with disrupted skull lymphoid structures had much more aggressive tumors and lower survival rates than control mice.
However, mice given a mix of three immune-boosting proteins showed stronger immune responses from their skull lymphoids, fighting off their cancer more effectively and significantly increasing their survival.
Of course, findings in mice don't necessarily translate to humans, but the researchers say that follicular T cells have previously been detected in the bone marrow of human skulls, which could be a clue that these structures are also hiding in our own heads.
If so, it could eventually mark a major improvement in how we fight brain cancer: A hydrogel injected under the scalp is far less invasive than full brain surgery to remove tumors.
"The finding fundamentally changes our current understanding of neuroimmunology," says Kipnis.
"Knowing that the brain relies on first responders in the surrounding skull for defense has the potential to change how we think about developing therapies for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, long COVID, and many others that have an immune component to them.
"Such therapies could access these immune hubs directly through the skull, without major peripheral side effects."
The research was published in the journal Nature.
summary: Biologists at Washington University School of Medicine have identified a new immune organ inside the skull bone marrow of mice, with signs suggesting humans have them too. These structures act as specialized training camps for immune cells, functioning as a security station to fight early-stage brain cancer. Researchers successfully used immune-boosting treatments via the skull in mice to improve survival rates against glioma, potentially offering less invasive treatment avenues for various neurological conditions.
key_points: Washington University researchers discovered a new immune organ inside the skull bone marrow.
The organ acts like a germinal center to train immune cells on the front lines to defend the brain.
Disrupting these skull structures in mice led to more aggressive brain tumors and lower survival rates.
Applying immune-boosting compounds under the scalp helped mice fight off cancer more effectively.
Researchers found clues that similar structures exist in human skulls, which could lead to less invasive brain cancer therapies.

title: The blood pressure mistakes cardiologists wish you’d stop making
author: Ella Nunn
content:
![Prof Tony Heagerty in his office](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735395_17841049377242_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqe8exRwkrG0gUQzS_A7vs-NHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Prof Tony Heagerty in his office](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735395_17841049377242_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqe8exRwkrG0gUQzS_A7vs-NHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
High blood pressure is one of medicine’s greatest paradoxes. It is among the leading preventable risk factors for heart disease, stroke and premature death worldwide, yet it rarely causes symptoms. As a result, many people do not realise they have the condition until it has already begun damaging the blood vessels supplying the heart, brain and kidneys.
Around one in three adults in the UK – an estimated 16 million people – have high blood pressure, and many are completely unaware of it.
The encouraging news is that there is plenty we can do to reduce our risk and keep our blood pressure under control. Here, five leading cardiologists share the most common blood pressure mistakes they see in midlife – and the simple changes that can make a real difference.
Ignoring heavy snoring
Normally, both blood pressure and heart rate fall by around 10 to 20 per cent during sleep. Known as the “nocturnal dip”, this gives the heart and blood vessels a chance to rest and recover overnight.
However, heavy snoring or obstructive sleep apnoea interrupts this recovery process. “The muscles in the throat relax too much, blocking the airway and depriving the body of oxygen, causing repeated awakenings throughout the night and preventing this normal overnight blood pressure dip,” says Dr Teresa Castiello, consultant cardiologist and founder of MIAL Healthcare.
![A portrait of Dr Teresa Castiello, consultant cardiologist and founder of MIAL Healthcare](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/14/TELEMMGLPICT000495192097_17840403072761_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq4GoSUj5tx--cOXjJHDSbw2mfEaXzUGjZTlLbjM4Zpow.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“When blood pressure and heart rate remain elevated overnight, it can increase the risk of high blood pressure and other health issues including heart failure and even dementia,” she explains.
If you or your partner snores heavily, it’s worth getting it checked rather than dismissing it as an inevitable part of ageing. Obstructive sleep apnoea is often highly treatable with airway devices such as CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) machines and lifestyle measures including weight loss and, for some people, changing sleep position.
Treating sleep apnoea consistently can help lower blood pressure and reduce strain on the cardiovascular system over time.
Only checking your blood pressure at weekends
Many of us are familiar with “white coat syndrome”, when blood pressure temporarily spikes because of anxiety in the GP’s office. It’s why doctors often advise measuring blood pressure at home over several days, to build a more accurate picture of cardiovascular health.
But if you only reach for the monitor when you’re relaxed at the weekend or at the end of the day, you could be missing stress-related rises in blood pressure during the working week.
“Some people develop high blood pressure at work or in everyday life when they are stressed, which may not show up at the doctor’s surgery or if they only measure their blood pressure at the weekend or in the evening,” says Dr Ali Khavandi, consultant interventional cardiologist at the Royal United Hospital Bath NHS Foundation Trust.
![Dr Ali Khavandi, a consultant cardiologist at the Royal United Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/14/TELEMMGLPICT000495192125_17840403099410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqHqEqWIQYN_HlsJ_HcWHEJEgS7S-ukhk48w-_KmtyACY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“This weekend-only approach creates a ‘best-case scenario’ measurement, hiding stress-related rises in blood pressure that may otherwise go unnoticed,” he explains. “It prevents you from seeing how your daily job strain impacts your cardiovascular system.”
Because high blood pressure rarely causes symptoms, doctors look for patterns over time rather than relying on isolated readings.
Relying on alcohol to relax
So many of us reach for a glass of wine at the end of a stressful working day, forgetting the impact on our heart health.
“High blood pressure and alcohol are best friends,” says Dr Khavandi. “The relationship between alcohol and blood pressure is dose-dependent, meaning the more you drink the greater the impact,” adds Professor Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, where he runs a hypertension service. “It’s also a risk factor for stroke, independent of its effects on blood pressure.”
![A portrait of Prof Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735504_17841049376101_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Some studies suggest that even moderate alcohol consumption may contribute to small rises in blood pressure over time in some people. If you drink more than two alcoholic drinks a day, halving your intake can produce clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure, with the greatest benefit seen among heavier drinkers, according to research published in The Lancet.
“If you find yourself reaching for alcohol as a way to relax, try experimenting with other ways to switch off,” Prof Heagerty advises, “whether that is taking a long bath, going for a walk, or cooking a new recipe”.
Thinking exercise makes you immune
In her clinic, Dr Castiello recalls shocked patients saying: “But doctor, I am highly active, I eat exceptionally well, I do yoga – how can my blood pressure be an issue?” She says: “This highlights the misconception that hypertension is exclusively a third-age affliction or something that only affects sedentary individuals.”
In reality, ageing itself – alongside age-related hormonal changes, including the menopause in women and declining testosterone levels in some men – can contribute to rising blood pressure, even among people who are otherwise healthy and active. A healthy lifestyle still helps, Dr Castiello stresses, but at these transition points, it isn’t always enough on its own.
“Oestrogen naturally helps keep blood vessels flexible and dilated,” explains Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew’s Hospital. “As its levels decline during menopause, blood vessels can become stiffer and less able to relax, leading to higher blood pressure.”
![Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew's Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495329297_17841272780770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqOfbQuL7vt0ioTIEx8Tqi0Ad_otF3axIcGgYHqpm5-IA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“Reducing the salt in your diet, maintaining a healthy weight and walking at a brisk pace for at least 150 minutes per week can all help to manage this risk,” Dr Laskar says.
Shrugging off “borderline” blood pressure
While it’s tempting to shrug off a slightly elevated reading as “fine”, you do so at your peril, says Dr Castiello: “This is a dangerous and pervasive myth”.
While a clinic reading of 125/85 mmHg isn’t considered hypertension, it does not mean you are risk-free. “Slightly elevated readings can still signal an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease, particularly when combined with other factors such as age, family history, smoking, excess weight or diabetes,” explains Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital.
The latest European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines, published in 2024, introduced a new category of “elevated blood pressure”, covering clinic readings between 120-139 mmHg systolic or 70-89 mmHg diastolic. This differs from current UK NICE guidance, which uses different thresholds and recommends confirming hypertension with home or ambulatory monitoring. Meanwhile, in the UK, an average home blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg or higher is considered high.
![Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495297892_17841049354400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqT1yghX8zbx7fxQBY89c64Yh-1OKnoApjyaprnWnv9tw.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The good news is that this stage offers an opportunity to act. Improving your diet, exercising regularly, maintaining a healthy weight and reducing alcohol intake can all help prevent blood pressure from rising further and reduce future cardiovascular risk.
Missing the salt hiding in everyday foods
When we think of salty foods, most of us know the obvious culprits: bacon, crisps, takeaways and adding salt at the table. But plenty of everyday foods – including those with a healthy reputation – can also contain surprising amounts of salt, says Dr Wamil.
Canned soups, wholemeal bread, breakfast cereals, some low-fat cheeses – including feta and reduced-fat cheddar – and smoked fish such as kippers and smoked salmon can all contain significant amounts of sodium, which is the main component of salt. Manufacturers often add it to preserve food and enhance flavour.
A typical serving of smoked salmon can provide around 1.5 to 2g of salt – roughly 30 per cent of the recommended maximum daily intake of 6g for an adult.
Over time, eating too much salt can “cause the body to retain more water, increasing total blood volume and forcing the heart to work harder to pump blood while simultaneously stiffening blood vessel walls”, Dr Wamil says.
The best way to manage this risk is to pay closer attention to the foods you eat regularly. UK guidance recommends that adults consume no more than 6g of salt a day (around one teaspoon). Check food labels, choose fresh or frozen whole foods where possible, and look for products labelled “low salt”, “low sodium” or “no added salt”.
Forgetting the damage it can do to your brain
Many people think of high blood pressure as a problem that mainly affects the heart. But persistent hypertension can also take a toll on the brain, increasing the risk of stroke, cognitive decline and dementia.
Dr Khavandi compares undiagnosed high blood pressure to “leaving a tap on and letting it drip in the background for a long period”. Over time, this constant pressure can silently damage the small blood vessels that supply the brain.
“This vascular damage contributes to vascular dementia and is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease,” he explains. While some of this damage may be irreversible, the good news is that controlling blood pressure can significantly reduce the risk of stroke and is associated with a lower risk of cognitive decline over time.
Ultimately, the advice remains reassuringly simple: maintain a healthy weight, stay physically active, eat a balanced diet, limit salt and alcohol, prioritise good sleep and have your blood pressure checked regularly.
