summary: High blood pressure is a major, often symptomless risk factor for heart disease, stroke, and dementia, affecting millions of adults who remain unaware of it. Leading cardiologists highlight several common mistakes people make regarding their blood pressure in midlife, such as ignoring heavy snoring, only testing on weekends, relying on alcohol to relax, and overlooking hidden salt in everyday foods. Making simple lifestyle adjustments and monitoring blood pressure consistently can significantly reduce cardiovascular and cognitive risks over time.
key_points: Ignoring heavy snoring or sleep apnoea prevents the normal overnight drop in blood pressure, increasing long-term cardiovascular risks.
Checking blood pressure only on relaxed weekends can hide stress-related spikes that occur during the working week.
Regularly relying on alcohol to relax contributes to dose-dependent increases in blood pressure and stroke risk.
Being active and healthy does not make individuals immune to hypertension, as age-related hormonal changes like menopause can cause blood vessels to stiffen.
Everyday foods like bread, breakfast cereals, and canned soups often contain surprising amounts of hidden salt that force the heart to work harder.

title: Jeremy Clarkson says men have lost the right to prostate cancer testing – the truth is a bit more nuanced than that
author: Justin Stebbing
content:
People are up in arms about changes to the prostate cancer screening guidelines in the UK.
TV personality Jeremy Clarkson wrote on X: “Until last week, men over 50 were entitled to a free PSA prostate cancer check. But the government has now decided to withdraw that right. I cannot for the life of me work out what their reasoning might be.”
Former prime minister David Cameron, who credits the test with catching his own cancer, called the changes “yet another step backwards”.
The fear is easy to understand. Why make it harder to get a simple blood test that could spot a deadly cancer before symptoms appear?
At the centre of the row is the PSA, or prostate-specific antigen, test. PSA is a protein made by the prostate, and prostate cancer can cause levels of it in the blood to rise.
Prostate cancer is much easier to treat before it spreads, so finding it early sounds like an obvious win. But PSA has a fundamental limitation: it is not actually a cancer test. High PSA levels can be caused by cancer, but also by an enlarged prostate, inflammation or infection. And some men with prostate cancer have normal PSA levels.
There’s another problem. Not all prostate cancers behave in the same way. Some grow quickly and can become life threatening. Others grow so slowly that they would never cause symptoms. If we test millions of healthy men, we will inevitably find some of these harmless cancers. This is known as overdiagnosis.
But once someone is told they have cancer, choosing not to treat it can be difficult for both patients and doctors. Treatment with surgery or radiotherapy can cure prostate cancer, but it can also cause urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction and other lasting side-effects. This is why the UK has never had a national PSA screening programme for all men over 50.
Screening programmes are not judged simply on whether they find cancers earlier. They also have to save enough lives to outweigh the harms caused by testing large numbers of healthy people.
Large trials of PSA screening have shown that it can reduce deaths from prostate cancer, but at the cost of substantial overdiagnosis. For that reason, the UK National Screening Committee still does not recommend routine screening for all men.
What changed in the guidance?
Until recently, NHS guidance under the Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme stated that men aged 50 and over without symptoms could ask for a PSA test after discussing the potential benefits and harms with their GP. That programme has now been retired.
Men can still ask for a PSA test, but GPs now have clearer discretion over whether to offer one, based on a man’s personal risk factors. The government says this clarifies existing guidance rather than taking away anyone’s right to be tested.
Critics argue that, in practice, it creates an additional barrier between an informed man and a test he previously expected to receive.
At the same time, the UK is starting to focus screening on people at the highest risk. From 2027, men aged 45 to 61 who carry harmful BRCA mutations – a gene change more commonly associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer – are planned to be offered PSA screening every two years.
Screening men most likely to develop prostate cancer makes sense because it increases the chances of finding dangerous cancers while reducing unnecessary diagnoses.
That raises the question of other high-risk groups. Black men have approximately twice the lifetime risk of developing prostate cancer as white men, while having a father or brother with the disease also increases risk. But there still isn’t enough evidence to justify a national screening programme for these groups.
![A phial of blood with 'PSA test' written on the label.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/754584/original/file-20260818-50-p3y4x7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
A major UK study called Transform is testing whether MRI scans, genetic information and other risk-based approaches can do a better job of identifying dangerous prostate cancers. That’s important because diagnosing prostate cancer has changed considerably since the early PSA screening trials.
A man with a raised PSA can now undergo a type of scan called a multiparametric MRI before biopsy. MRI can identify suspicious areas of the prostate, allow biopsies to be targeted and help some men avoid a biopsy altogether.
And if a small, low-risk cancer is found, doctors increasingly use “active surveillance” – monitoring it carefully rather than immediately operating or giving radiotherapy. These advances could reduce two of the biggest problems that made PSA screening so controversial in the first place.
So the claim that men over 50 have simply been denied PSA testing is too strong. They can still ask for a test, although access now more explicitly depends on a GP’s judgment. But the anger surrounding the change reflects a genuine scientific and ethical tension.
For someone such as Cameron, whose symptomless cancer was discovered through PSA testing, the benefit of early detection is intensely personal and obvious. Screening policy has to answer a harder question: what happens when the same test is offered to millions of healthy men?
The real debate, therefore, should not be about whether early diagnosis saves lives – it can. It is about whether we can find the prostate cancers that need to be found while leaving the harmless ones alone. PSA by itself has never been very good at doing that. An interesting question now is whether MRI scans, genetic risk scores and better monitoring have improved diagnosis enough to tip the balance in favour of wider screening.
summary: Recent changes to UK prostate cancer guidance have sparked public debate, with figures like Jeremy Clarkson and David Cameron criticizing the shift. While the retired Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme allowed men over 50 to request a PSA test after discussing risks with a GP, current guidelines give GPs clearer discretion based on personal risk factors. The UK does not have a routine national screening programme for all men due to limitations of the PSA test, which include high rates of false positives and harmless overdiagnoses that lead to difficult treatment side-effects.
key_points: Jeremy Clarkson and David Cameron criticized recent changes to UK prostate cancer guidance regarding PSA tests.
The PSA test is not a direct cancer test and can result in overdiagnosis of harmless cancers, leading to unnecessary and harmful treatments.
Men over 50 can still request a PSA test, but updated guidance gives GPs clearer discretion based on personal risk factors.
The UK plans to offer targeted PSA screening starting in 2027 to men aged 45 to 61 carrying harmful BRCA mutations.
Advances like MRI scans and active surveillance are helping doctors better identify dangerous cancers and monitor low-risk ones.

title: 'I was diagnosed with cancer at 21 - now I face an £8,000 bill to become a mum'
author: Laura Trimble; Vanessa Taaffe
content:
A cancer survivor who underwent urgent treatment at 21 is facing an £8,000 bill to preserve her chance of becoming a mum.
Erin Lavery, from Cambuslang, was diagnosed with stage three Hodgkin’s Lymphoma aged just 21 after having her symptoms dismissed for over a year.
She was advised to begin treatment immediately due to the late diagnosis, but later discovered she had gone through menopause and was told it was too late for egg freezing to be funded by the NHS.
The Scottish Government says patients are assessed on a case-by-case basis and will shortly outline details of a new review of IVF services.
Now 23 and cancer-free, Erin is pushing for change to ensure other young women can still have children after cancer treatment.
“I always wanted to be a mum, so as soon as I could begin those investigations, that’s what I did,” she told STV News.
“I can’t describe the emotions it’s brought up going through this. It’s already isolating being a young person going through cancer, but infertility as well; it doesn’t need to be this difficult.
“If the funding is there before your cancer treatment, it should be there after.”
Erin was diagnosed in August 2024 after a year of escalating symptoms, which doctors attributed to low iron.
The young nail technician had been suffering from a persistent cough, shortness of breath, and extreme fatigue before being sent for tests.
A biopsy revealed she had Stage 3 Hodgkin’s Lymphoma, and she was forced to start treatment immediately.
She had gone through six months of chemotherapy and a month of radiotherapy and is now clear of cancer.
Earlier this year, further tests found there was a chance she could preserve her eggs and have a child in the future.
However, because fertility preservation would take place after her cancer treatment rather than before it, she was told it would not be funded by the NHS and would instead need to be self-funded at a cost of around £8,000.
“I’m lucky enough that my family are able to help me fund this, but I can’t stop thinking about people who don’t have that option, or even to find that amount of money.
“It’s so disheartening. I’m now at this stage where I’m recovering and getting myself back, and to be hit with this feels huge.
“It’s taken me a while to get a good bit of myself back and recover from treatment.
“Fighting for funding and trying to change this is exhausting.”
![Erin has returned to work as a nail technician](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/4f973ffc91d5554bf4ea35157235a60d-1786977438.jpeg) STV News
She’s speaking out to raise awareness and criticise what she describes as an “outdated” policy affecting young women like herself.
“A large part of this seems to be an area missed and not looked over. These policies that need a second look.
” If I need to be the one to change that, I’m going to do it.
“It’s upsetting so many cancer survivors find themselves in this situation and are left on their own to navigate it.”
Public health minister Maree Todd said: “Guidance on fertility preservation has been developed by clinical experts and makes clear that special consideration by health boards should be done on a case-by-case basis, to cover the whole range of possible conditions and individual circumstances where fertility preservation might be considered.
“I am sympathetic to the calls from this campaign and am keen to hear more from Erin about her experience. The Scottish Government will shortly outline details of a new review of IVF services, which will look at the experiences of accessing IVF services.
“I greatly admire the strength and resilience shown by Erin as she has documented her cancer journey online and I thank her for the sharing her personal experience and the work she is doing to advocate for more support for cancer survivors.”

summary: Erin Lavery, a 23-year-old cancer survivor from Cambuslang, is facing an £8,000 self-funded bill to preserve her fertility after her urgent cancer treatment induced menopause at age 21. Because her fertility preservation procedures would happen after her cancer treatment rather than before, the NHS denied funding under current policies. Now cancer-free, Erin is campaigning to change what she views as an outdated system to help other young survivors.
key_points: Erin Lavery was diagnosed with stage three Hodgkin's Lymphoma at age 21 after her symptoms were initially dismissed for over a year.
Due to the need for immediate cancer treatment, she underwent six months of chemotherapy and a month of radiotherapy, which caused her to go through menopause.
She was denied NHS funding for egg freezing because the procedure would take place after her cancer treatment instead of before, resulting in an £8,000 out-of-pocket cost.
The Scottish Government stated that patients are assessed on a case-by-case basis and announced plans to outline details of a new review of IVF services.
Erin is actively speaking out to raise awareness and advocate for policy changes to support young cancer survivors facing infertility.

title: The simple Birmingham home test that could be 'amazing' for bladder cancer patients
author: Joanne Writtle
content:
![Trevor is standing in his back garden, smiling into camera. He is wearing a blue patterned shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/6ffc/live/41e410d0-94d0-11f1-8189-057951e10a11.jpg)
Trevor Field was first diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2013 and has to be monitored regularly
- Published
Trevor Field knows how uncomfortable tests for bladder cancer can be.
In the 13 years since the 81-year-old was diagnosed, he has had more cystoscopies than he can count.
The procedure involves inserting a camera into the bladder and he has to have these every six to 12 months, to make sure his cancer has not returned.
But he could eventually benefit from a simple urine test at home instead: "That would be tremendous."
The test is currently being offered to new patients in Coventry and Leicester along with parts of Wales and will lead to faster treatment and cut waiting lists, according to the West Midlands Cancer Alliance.
Trevor, from Tipton, said that would be "amazing" and that the procedures he has "aren't the easiest thing" for some people.
"I can understand some people would get embarrassed as most of the staff when I go are female and I can understand some people would find that difficult," he added.
![Dr Omer smiles into camera, standing outside the hospital entrance. He is wearing a white shirt and blue jacket.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4212/live/534bba20-94d6-11f1-9229-0f9d840c190e.jpg)
Altan Omer said the new tests had a high degree of accuracy
When he got his diagnosis in 2013, he had to wait about six weeks for the test and said being able to carry out a simple test at home should help cut waiting times.
"The sooner they find you have something, the better the outcome," Trevor said.
"Mine was caught early enough; if I had not gone when I did and it had gone through my bladder, it could have spread to other parts of my body."
The idea of the new tests is an exciting one for Altan Omer.
He is a consultant urologist at the University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust as well as being chair of the alliance's urology expert advisory group.
"We will stop performing unnecessary tests which can harm patients," he told me.
"It has got a great accuracy. It's got a sensitivity of 92% in detecting bladder cancer and it also has got a high accuracy at ruling out bladder cancer of 99.3%."
![Three people wearing white coats work in a lab.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/30df/live/a6df9280-94d9-11f1-8a7b-e7300179227e.jpg)
The new test was developed at a diagnostics company in Quinton, Birmingham
The urine test can provide a result within two weeks. The NHS requirement is for patients to have a diagnosis within 28 days of their referral.
But figures from the West Midlands Cancer Alliance show nearly a third of patients waited more than six weeks for a cystoscopy in West Midlands hospitals in 2025.
That compares to just over a quarter nationally. The waiting list in Coventry was 66%.
The academic research for the test took place over a decade at the University of Birmingham and was then developed over the last two years at Nonacus, a diagnostic company in Quinton, on the outskirts of the city.
"Currently there are about 320,000 people in the UK that have blood in their urine and that's a key risk factor for bladder cancer," the firm's chief executive Jeff Bousfield said.
"When patients come in for an invasive procedure today to see if there is cancer present, only around seven per cent of those tested have cancer.
"It means that in effect you have all of these people in a waiting list that are actually cancer free that are taking up space I suppose from testing those that actually do have cancer and need to be treated more quickly."
![Jeff Bousfield is wearing a white shirt. He is standing in the lab smiling into camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2aae/live/0a41f740-94db-11f1-8a7b-e7300179227e.jpg)
Jeff Bousfield, chief executive of Nonacus, said it was "rewarding to see something developed here making a real difference"
Currently the test is for new patients with possible symptoms.
But trials are going on in the hope of rolling it out within the next two years for people like Trevor, who need monitoring.
"If they can, just by simply taking a sample of your urine, tell you that there's nothing to worry about, that would be amazing," he said.
The new test will be available in all West Midlands hospitals by next April after it was commissioned by the West Midlands Cancer Alliance.
Nonacus said it was working towards wider national access and was in discussions with a number of NHS trusts.
The government was determined to make use of new technology to improve cancer treatments in England, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said.
"While NHS organisations make decisions based on the needs of their local population, we've set up a programme to identify new technologies that have the potential to benefit both NHS patients and services," they added.
summary: A new home urine test for bladder cancer is being introduced for new patients in parts of England and Wales, offering an alternative to invasive cystoscopies. Developed in Birmingham and featuring high accuracy rates, the test aims to reduce waiting lists and speed up diagnoses. Trials are also underway to eventually monitor patients who have already had cancer.
key_points: The new home urine test has a 92% sensitivity in detecting bladder cancer and a 99.3% accuracy in ruling it out.
The test was developed at a diagnostic company in Birmingham following academic research at the University of Birmingham.
It is currently being offered to new patients in Coventry, Leicester, and parts of Wales, with availability in all West Midlands hospitals expected by next April.
Trials are exploring whether the test can be used within two years to monitor patients who require regular follow-ups.

title: Cheadle mental health wards ordered to improve upgraded to 'good'
author: Lynette Horsburgh
content:
![A nurse is moving a hospital chair along a corridor while two other nurses attend to paperwork](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/5e59/live/8480fb90-9b3a-11f1-adfc-97cecc6f1ad1.png)
Inspectors carried out tours of two wards as part of the inspection
- Published
Child and adolescent mental health wards at a Greater Manchester hospital that had been ordered to improve has been rated as "good" by health inspectors.
The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of the service at Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards after an inspection in April.
The hospital, run by Affinity Healthcare Limited, provides a range of inpatient mental health services for young people between 11-17 and adults. The inspection followed the receipt of information of concern, the CQC said.
CQC inspectors found the hospital had made necessary improvements and was now only in breach of one regulation related to safe care and treatment.
At the previous inspection, inspectors found five breaches of regulation.
At the time of this latest review, the CQC said there were six young people admitted to the main ward and one young person in long-term segregation on another ward, which was not in general use.
Inspectors carried out a tour of the Woodlands and Featherstone wards as well as the clinic room and the ward seclusion suite.
The CQC upgraded its rating for how responsive and well-led the service was from "required improvement" to "good", and has again rated how effective and caring the service is as good.
The report found:
- Staff treated young people with compassion and kindness, respected their privacy and dignity and involved them and their families in planning their care
- Leaders had a good understanding of how the ward was run and were visible and approachable to both staff and young people
- The ward met people's needs well as staff, managed people's cases effectively, they did not move young people between wards unnecessarily and they supported people to leave hospital as soon as they were well enough to do so
- Staff supported young people with discharge planning, working closely with community teams and commissioners to help them move on to suitable placements.
- Staff assessed young people's physical and mental health needs thoroughly on admission and reviewed their care plans regularly to reflect any changes.
However the inspectors also noted:
- Staff did not always store medicines safely, putting some young people at risk of receiving medicines that were out of date or had not been stored at the correct temperature
- Staff did not always update risk records quickly enough after incidents so important information about a young person's specific risks did not always appear in their care plan
- Some issues with maintenance and infection prevention and control issues in the care environment
The CQC has asked Affinity Healthcare Limited for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment.
The health watchdog's overall rating at Cheadle Royal Hospital has remained the same as "requires improvement".

summary: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of child and adolescent mental health wards at Cheadle Royal Hospital to 'good' following an inspection in April. Inspectors found that the hospital had addressed most previous concerns, reducing its regulatory breaches from five to one, though minor issues related to medicine storage, risk records, and maintenance remain. Despite the upgraded wards, the hospital's overall rating continues to be 'requires improvement'.
key_points: Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards were upgraded from 'requires improvement' to 'good' by the CQC.
The hospital reduced its regulatory breaches from five down to one concerning safe care and treatment.
Inspectors noted that staff treated young people compassionately and conducted thorough physical and mental health assessments.
Areas of concern included the unsafe storage of some medicines, delayed updates to risk records, and minor maintenance and infection control issues.
The CQC requested an action plan from Affinity Healthcare Limited to address the remaining concerns, while the hospital's overall rating remains 'requires improvement'.

title: You can call ADHD whatever you like — I still have to live with it
author: Jessica Lindsay
content:
![Max Pemberton on The Great ADHD Myth?](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image003-4ab6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
In Channel 4’s new documentary, The Great ADHD Myth?, psychiatrist Max Pemberton seeks to determine whether it’s ‘a genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or a social construct.’
Having spent the five years since my own diagnosis fielding similar bad faith questions — and given Pemberton has previously suggested that ADHD could be a ‘wildly overdiagnosed’ ‘fad’ — the resulting answer didn’t come as a shock.
Despite claiming to take a ‘science-led approach’, the show appeared to use the same carefully-chosen sceptics and cherry-picked evidence as every other so-called investigation into the ‘rise’ of neurodiversity.
It’s all pretty inflammatory.
One of the experts featured called medication prescribed to treat ADHD ‘slow-release cocaine’ (as someone who’s taken both, I can confirm that’s complete nonsense), while others said it was ‘worse’ than corporal punishment or likened it to chemical castration.
What felt especially unique about the documentary though, is how it merged these provocative statements with elements of truth, latching their central thesis onto legitimate concerns about everything from big pharma to ultra-processed foods to smartphone addiction.
Personally, I’m inclined to trust the World Health Organization, the NHS and NICE in their classifications of ADHD as a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder.
But let’s for a minute assume Max Pemberton and co are correct and it is in fact a product of modern society — when people are suffering, who’s helped by proving that point?
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-925684848-3e6d.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The thread that runs through the hour-long show is an experiment where a 10-year-old boy with ADHD, Mason, is taken off his meds in favour of daily yoga, woodland walks, diet changes and screen time limits.
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
During the four-week trial, we’re told he’d become ‘more fun’ and ‘a proper character’.
When his teacher reports that the year 6 pupil is struggling to concentrate or regulate his emotions during lessons, and was ‘easier to teach’ while medicated, it’s labelled as an ‘educational issue’.
At the end, Mason whoops with joy as his mum Shauna decides to keep him off the drugs for a longer period to avoid ‘dulling his sparkle to suit everyone else’.
It’s not until the credits roll that we find out he’s back on them after doing poorly in his exams.
In Pemberton’s view, this experiment (with the smallest possible sample size of one) raised some ‘profound philosophical and moral questions’ about neurodiversity.
In mine, it’s a clear example of the real world harms that can come from constantly questioning its very existence.
Ex-GP Iona Heath said on the show that if she was in charge, she’d ‘ban the label ADHD, straight off.’
‘I would stop medicating this group of people, then I would absolutely want to overhaul the education system for children to include many more creative activities and sporting activities,’ she added.
‘I think that would reveal an untapped reservoir of talent that we are currently drugging out of existence.’
Cool. If I could bake a cake filled with rainbows and smiles, everyone would eat it and be happy.
Until we build that utopia, Mason has to follow a set curriculum alongside the 30-odd other kids in his class in order to get the qualifications he needs to be a functioning member of society.
And I, along with the millions of adults with ADHD who work in offices, have to sit at a desk and concentrate for eight hours a day to earn a living.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2148402031-9f6b.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
It’s not that I don’t agree with any of the points raised in the documentary around how modernity and diagnoses seem to go hand in hand. In fact, I’m a firm believer that in another time, or even a less rigid class system, the hyperfocus and creativity of neurodivergence would be seen as assets rather than problems.
I’m sure our collective need for instant gratification isn’t helping the symptoms of ADHD either, and we could all benefit from touching a little more grass, eating a little less sugar, and spending a lot less time doomscrolling.
The reality of life today, though, is that we rely on phones to do most things, from taxes to communicating with loved ones, working long hours at increasingly insecure jobs, often in built-up areas.
- 
	![Woman massaging her leg because of leg muscle cramps. Muscle pain or leg pain while sleeping in the bed. High quality photo](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308652563-f573.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- A man at church told me about his fetish — now I fulfil his fantasy for £120 an hour
- This is what Brits consider cheating — men and women have very different views
- Your star sign's daily horoscope for August 19, 2026
If you want to get by in a world where productivity is king, you need to conform to a certain extent. For those of us with ADHD, medication is the most accessible way to do that.
Perhaps, as Pemberton concludes, it is ‘dystopian’ to medicate children (albeit with drugs that have been safely used for decades) and to medicalise ‘normal’ behaviour instead of changing the society that deems it otherwise.
What scares me more is that research shows someone with diagnosed ADHD has a seven to nine-year lower life expectancy, not to mention a higher risk of substance abuse issues, unemployment and even suicide.
That is the reality we are doing our best to deal with in the here and now. Thinking that arguing the semantics of our condition or demonising medication many of us find life-changing will help improve our situation would be the biggest myth of all.

The author, who has ADHD, criticizes the program for using cherry-picked evidence and dangerous rhetoric against ADHD medication. While acknowledging modern societal pressures that exacerbate symptoms, the author argues that medication remains essential for navigating a productivity-driven world.

The author emphasizes that medication is a crucial, accessible tool for individuals with ADHD to function in a rigid, productivity-focused society.

title: Salmonella outbreak: What we know so far
author: Smitha Mundasd
content:
![A carton of eggs are in focus, with a hand picking up on egg.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/9b42/live/0e674fe0-9bdf-11f1-ba30-ddd78081057f.jpg)
- Published
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has recently declared a national outbreak, external of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill with the bug.
Although not yet proven, imported eggs or dishes containing them are the leading suspects as to the cause.
Evidence also suggests people caught the bug while eating out, rather than at home - with catering and food services such as restaurants, cafes or take-aways likely to play a part.
But there is still a lot to be discovered.
What do we know and what questions remain?
What is salmonella and how do you catch it?
Salmonella are a family of bacteria that typically live harmlessly in the digestive tract of animals including cattle, pigs and chicken - which is why eggs and poultry are among foods commonly associated with the infection.
The bacteria are shed in animal faeces.
You can catch the bug by:
- eating contaminated food that has not been cooked properly
- drinking contaminated water
- coming into contact with infected animals
- cross contamination after mixing raw and cooked food in the kitchen for example
Person-to-person spread is rare.
What are the symptoms?
Signs to watch out for include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.
In most cases people recover without further help but older people, babies and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk of severe disease.
Hospital care with fluids and sometimes antibiotics can help in these cases.
Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.
Can cooking eggs get rid of salmonella?
Yes, cooking eggs and other food thoroughly can prevent infection.
Other ways to protect yourself include washing your hands before preparing food, after using the bathroom and after contact with animals.
In the current outbreak most infections do not seem to arise from food that has cooked at home.
The Food Standards Agency, external has recently issued guidance to catering businesses on the storage and handling of eggs.
Where is the outbreak happening?
The majority of recent cases - 199 of the 207 - have been in England, including 47 in London and 38 in Yorkshire and Humber.
There have been six cases in Scotland, one in Wales and another in Northern Ireland.
While the cases are spread out, scientists used a type of comprehensive genetic fingerprinting called whole-genome sequencing, which revealed the bugs involved are all closely related.
Tests show there are only a handful of differences in their DNA sequences, which indicate the infections are part of the same outbreak, with a common source.
![A bowl with a hard boiled egg sliced in half, with salad leaves, broccoli and cucumber slices.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/0b2c/live/6ba6ecb0-9bdf-11f1-ba30-ddd78081057f.jpg)
Why are imported eggs considered the most likely source?
Genetic testing of the bacteria suggests there are similarities with a previous outbreak involving imported eggs.
UKHSA experts questioned 114 people involved in the current outbreak and their answers indicate that eggs provide the "strongest signal" or clue.
Some 24 cases had links to five businesses (which have not been named), with 11 people reporting they ate dishes containing eggs.
Investigations suggest these premises may use eggs that are supplied from multiple sources, including imported sources.
In some localities there have been questions over hygiene practices.
"At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry," the UKHSA says.
Which eggs should you buy?
Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the Food Security Agency, says the standard advice remains unchanged - thoroughly cooked eggs that are handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.
Infants, young children, those who are pregnant and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme.
People who are immunocompromised should follow their doctor's advice.
Meanwhile Dr Kathleen O'Reilly at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine recommends checking out food hygiene ratings when deciding on cafes or restaurants.
How are British eggs kept safe?
The vaccination of commercial hens against common salmonella strains, which began in the mid-1990s in the UK, has been a "major public health success" and has "substantially reduced egg-associated salmonella infections," according to Dr Charlotte Hammer at the University of Cambridge.
Another quality control measure is the British Lion Scheme, launched in 1998.
Any suppliers of eggs given the British Lion mark have to stick to a strict code that covers the vaccinating of hens, regular testing and a passport system to make sure hens are traceable.
Paul Wigley, professor in animal microbial ecosystems at the Bristol Veterinary School, says improved surveillance and detection has also helped.
"However, we do still import a large number of eggs and egg product, and salmonella could be contained within these because the countries in which they're produced don't use that same level of control," he added.
Meanwhile, Mark Williams, chairman of the British Egg Industry Council, said food businesses which import eggs should check their supply lines for vaccination information and that all the food safety checks have been done.
What do we still not know?
Health experts still need to confirm that eggs are the source and the UKHSA is continuing to interview people confirmed to have caught the bug.
Local authorities will be carrying out tests on businesses that are likely to be involved as well as carrying out some opportunistic testing.
Experts will also need to look at the whole supply chain, investigating where the eggs or egg products have been eaten, supplied stored and farmed, for example.
Once they have enough information an important step would be to limit further infections.
The exact source and country of origin will need to be traced.
One challenge is that when a business imports a large number of eggs, they can come from mixed sources.
The UKHSA has alerted other countries about this outbreak so they can check for any genetically similar infections.
And while salmonella infections occur every year in the UK, outbreaks that grow this quickly are relatively unusual, according to Dr Gauri Godbole at the UKHSA, so scientists will want to examine the factors that led to this situation.
summary: The UK Health Security Agency has declared a national salmonella outbreak resulting in one death and hundreds of illnesses, primarily across England. Genetic testing links the cases to a common source, with imported eggs and catering services currently suspected by investigators. While the exact source is still being confirmed, experts advise that thoroughly cooked eggs and those bearing specific British assurance marks remain safe.
key_points: A national salmonella outbreak has caused one death and hundreds of illnesses, with 199 of the 207 recent cases occurring in England.
Genetic fingerprinting indicates the infections are closely related and share a common source.
Imported eggs and dishes eaten at catering services and restaurants are the leading suspects, with no identified link to UK-produced eggs.
Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever, typically developing 12 to 72 hours after infection.
Health authorities and local officials are continuing to investigate the supply chain and trace the exact origin of the outbreak.

title: Caernarfon teen's ovarian cancer put her in menopause overnight
author: Danielle Herbert
content:
![Enlli Thompson posing for a selfie in a mirror. She is pouting and looking at the camera, with her phone in her right hand. She has a shaven head and is wearing a black dress with a white floral pattern.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1248/cpsprodpb/4c41/live/9f72a410-9006-11f1-9dfb-fd4408d16f2f.jpg)
Enlli froze seven eggs before having chemotherapy for stage 3 ovarian cancer
- Published
When Enlli Thompson's periods changed and she began experiencing excruciating pain at 19, she was told by doctors there was nothing wrong.
Her stomach issues and headaches were blamed on a bug or a urinary infection - even anxiety.
It was only after Enlli had further tests when a scan showed a cyst in her pelvis that the teenager from Caernarfon, Gwynedd, was given the devastating news she had ovarian cancer.
She would need a full hysterectomy to remove her womb, which would put her into immediate menopause, and means she is not able to have children.
But Enlli said her life had changed for the better.
"I used to be quiet and shy, but now I feel like I'm in a really good place," she said.
![Enlli Thompson is photographed in a hospital bed. She is wearing a grey vest top which is covered in a pattern of small black hearts. She is drinking a blue slush drink and holding a white and red straw. She looks at the camera, smiling and winking.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/c61d/live/b903a030-90bc-11f1-b8f3-bf6a2c059a9b.jpg)
Since entering surgical menopause, Enlli experiences symptoms including hot flushes, brain fog, joint and muscle pain and fatigue
Enlli started experiencing problems in 2024.
"My periods were changing, I was experiencing severe pain, but I was still being told I was fine," she said.
She described being "completely at a loss" and felt like she was "losing the plot".
But the pain became too much, and she visited A&E at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.
Scans revealed what was believed to be a cyst in her pelvic area, and she was placed on a medical plan to carefully monitor her condition, while continuing to work as a trainee mechanic.
"I was taking painkillers and working through the pain," Enlli said.
She then received a call from the hospital to return for further scans, and admitted: "My mind went straight to cancer."
Her worst fears were confirmed, and she was told she had stage 3 ovarian cancer, external, which meant it had spread beyond the pelvis.
"Being told that I wouldn't be able to have my own children, I broke down and cried," she said.
"I had so much support, but it was so difficult hearing those words."
But Enlli said: "In a strange way I was kind of relieved when they told me I had cancer.
"Just because then I had an answer, I had a treatment plan, I was going to get better."
Enlli received fertility treatment, and seven of her eggs were frozen.
She finished chemotherapy in September 2025, and passed her driving test a week later.
Enlli now experiences hot flushes, brain fog, joint and muscle pain and fatigue, and says it can be hard to identify which are from the menopause or effects of the chemotherapy.
"My memory is absolutely awful," she said.
![Enlli Thompson is photographed in hospital. She is smiling, looking at the camera with both thumbs up. She is wearing a hair net and a hospital gown.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/6eab/live/4a398350-9007-11f1-9dfb-fd4408d16f2f.jpg)
Enlli spent almost a year seeking answers before her life-changing diagnosis
Enlli believes her age meant ovarian cancer wasn't initially suspected, and while she doesn't blame doctors as it was such a rare case, she hopes lessons can be learnt from her story.
Every year, about 120 young women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer in the UK, and about one in 10,000 women experience the menopause in their teens.
"I want something to be done and for things to change so this doesn't happen to other young women, who are often not listened to, leading to important things like this being missed," she added.
Her cancer battle has given her a new sense of purpose and confidence, and Enlli raises awareness on social media as well as speaking publicly.
"I can't sit still, I love helping others and I'm much more confident than I was before," she said.
Enlli has also decided on a change of career and wants to work in cancer care to help others.
She decided to embrace her new look, by shaving her head after she lost some of her hair from chemotherapy.
"I rock the look," she said proudly.
"I may wear a wig if I'm dressing up, but usually I don't, and I get so many lovely compliments."
![Enlli Thompson taking part in  a fashion show for the charity, Tenovus Cancer Care. Her head is shaven and she is wearing a short sleeve orange dress. To her right is another young girl who is also taking part in the fashion show. She is wearing a brown jacket, white crop top and a purple floral skirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/7e8d/live/598b7030-9006-11f1-9dfb-fd4408d16f2f.jpg)
Enlli said she is "much more confident" since her cancer diagnosis and took part in a fashion show for the charity, Tenovus Cancer Care
Enlli's case is a "rare phenomenon", according to GP Dr Rebeccah Tomlinson.
She believes ovarian cancer can be hard to diagnose because the symptoms can be "vague".
"As a medical specialist, I would always say bloating is my red flag feature," she said.
"If somebody mentions bloating to me, I'm going to want to investigate because that is one of the most common signs of ovarian cancer and it often gets put down to irritable bowel syndrome because that's common."
Most people diagnosed with ovarian cancer are in their 50s or older, but it's becoming more common in teenagers and younger people, according to the Teenage Cancer Trust.
Cancer Research UK said about 120 young people aged 15 to 24 are diagnosed with ovarian cancer in the UK each year, and about five in Wales.
Tomlinson added: "It is sometimes possible to treat ovarian cancer without a full hysterectomy, depending on how quickly it's picked up and also what type of tumour it is.
"But unfortunately in younger people, sometimes cancers are more aggressive, so catching them early can sometimes be a lot more complicated."
What are the signs of ovarian cancer?
According to the NHS, external, symptoms include
- A swollen tummy or feeling bloated
- Pain or tenderness in your tummy or the area between your hips (pelvic pain)
- No appetite or feeling full quickly after eating
- An urgent need to pee or needing to pee more often
- Indigestion
- Constipation or diarrhoea
- Back pain
- Feeling tired all the time
- Losing weight without trying
- Unusual bleeding from the vagina, including between periods, heavier periods or after the menopause
What is the menopause?
Menopause, external is typically caused by a fall in hormone levels and usually affects women between the ages of 45 and 55, but it can happen earlier.
It is a natural biological stage where menstrual periods stop naturally.
According to Menopause Support, one in 10,000 women will experience menopause under the age of 20.

She is looking at the camera with her brown and blonde hair half tied up and half down. There is a cake to the left of her, which is a three tiered cake, in different shades of pink with flowers adorned on it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/a2ec/live/a08dc8d0-9b0e-11f1-bb80-c1b1e1adeea5.jpg)

summary: Nineteen-year-old Enlli Thompson from Caernarfon spent nearly a year being told nothing was wrong before she was diagnosed with stage 3 ovarian cancer. She underwent a full hysterectomy—which put her into immediate surgical menopause and prevented her from having children—along with fertility treatment to freeze seven of her eggs. Having finished chemotherapy in September 2025, Enlli now campaigns to raise awareness about young women's symptoms being dismissed and plans to pursue a career in cancer care.
key_points: Enlli Thompson experienced changing periods and severe pain at 19, but her symptoms were initially dismissed by doctors as a bug, infection, or anxiety.
A hospital scan revealed a pelvic cyst, leading to a diagnosis of stage 3 ovarian cancer.
She underwent a full hysterectomy that induced immediate menopause and left her unable to have children, though she froze seven eggs prior to treatment.
Enlli finished chemotherapy in September 2025 and now raises awareness on social media to help ensure other young women's symptoms are not missed.
About 120 young people aged 15 to 24 are diagnosed with ovarian cancer in the UK each year.

title: BBC’s Emma Barnett reveals she’s had hysterectomy ‘I never wanted to have’
author: Harriette Boucher
content:
BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed that she had to undergo a hysterectomy that she “didn’t want to have” as a result of her crippling endometriosis.
The 41-year-oldToday programme host said her symptoms became “a lot worse” in her final weeks of filming documentary Fighting Endometriosis, in which she discusses her life-long struggle with the condition.
Just two days before the documentary aired in June, Ms Barnett had to undergo a sudden and extensive endometriosis surgery, a hysterectomy to remove her womb and a gallbladder removal.
She wrote on Substack: “I felt blind-sided and robbed. Even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.
“But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have.”
![Ms Barnett first revealed her diagnosis in 2024](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/05/29/11/03/565532.jpeg)
Ms Barnett has frequently spoken out about the debilitating pain she experiences from endometriosis, a condition where tissue grows outside the uterus and causes swelling, bleeding, and severe pain during a period.
She said she did not want or plan to have her recent surgery, but said the situation became “urgent and non-negotiable”.
“I didn’t want this procedure because it’s major surgery. It’s frightening and a hard recovery - something I am living now. I didn’t want it because I wanted there to have been medicine or treatment to help my endometriosis. It felt and feels too extreme.
“Is such major surgery what anyone would ‘choose’? Yes, I officially and legally consented to the procedures - in so much as you can know what you are letting yourself in for.”
Ms Barnett said she did not “buy into the idea that the womb is sacred and at the heart of being a woman. I am still very much a woman and me.
“I am grateful to it because somehow it managed to help me have two children. Having your womb removed without having children if you wanted them is a totally different situation - one I must acknowledge.”
![Endometriosis costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/10/14/23/13082449-d089b217-2bf0-420e-8f16-e0c99a63d5fe.jpg)
Earlier this year, Ms Barnett spoke out about a “horrific” experience with endometriosis where she couldn’t “remember a single thing” about a radio broadcast after being hit with intense pain.
The presenter previously had a laparoscopy, a surgical procedure to surgically remove endometriosis, which she said was difficult to recover from, and provided no pain relief.
She returned to air on Wednesday morning after an 11-week recovery, which she described as “one of the most humbling experiences of my life.”
The cause of endometriosis is unknown and affects around one in 10 women, according to Endometriosis UK.
Some 1.5 million women in Britain suffer from the condition, which costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year in treatment, loss of work and healthcare costs.
summary: BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed she underwent an unexpected hysterectomy and gallbladder removal due to severe endometriosis. The 41-year-old broadcaster stated that while the surgery was urgent and non-negotiable, it was a procedure she never wanted and left her feeling blindsided. Barnett has since returned to work following an 11-week recovery period.
key_points: Emma Barnett underwent a sudden hysterectomy and gallbladder removal due to crippling endometriosis.
The 41-year-old presenter described the major surgery as a path she did not envision or want.
The procedure took place just two days before her documentary, Fighting Endometriosis, aired in June.
Barnett returned to the air on Wednesday after an 11-week recovery period.
Endometriosis affects approximately one in 10 women in the UK and costs the economy £8.2bn annually.

title: Prostate cancer can be diagnosed without invasive biopsy
author: Michael Searles
content:
Prostate cancer can be diagnosed without an invasive biopsy, a study has found.
Experts from University College London Hospitals (UCLH) said some men could have the disease detected through an MRI scan alone and not need procedures that carry a high risk of side effects.
Currently, NHS hospitals either give men with suspected prostate cancer an MRI, with doctors then deciding whether to take a biopsy, or they take a biopsy straight away.
But a study of 880 men found that using MRI scans and blood tests, as well as getting an expert opinion, detected the disease 99 per cent of the time.
Biopsies involve a small needle being put into the prostate to take a tissue sample.
There are two types of biopsy for prostate cancer, with needles inserted in different places. Both come with the risk of side effects, cancers being missed and the detection of cancers that may never need treating.
This is one of the reasons why health officials have not approved a wider screening using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood tests, because people whose results reveal suspected cancer have historically gone on to have biopsies.
But the new study found that some men could have their cancer diagnosed by MRI alone.
The findings could reignite calls for a screening programme.
The Telegraph has been campaigning for the rollout of targeted screening for thousands more men at increased risk, including black men and those with a family history of the disease.
Last week, this newspaper revealed that men aged over 50 are no longer entitled to a blood test to help identify the disease, with GPs deciding who receives one.
summary: A study of 880 men by experts at University College London Hospitals found that prostate cancer can be diagnosed using MRI scans, blood tests, and expert opinion without the need for an invasive biopsy. The findings show this non-invasive approach detected the disease 99 percent of the time, potentially avoiding the risks of side effects associated with tissue samples. This discovery could reignite calls for a wider targeted screening programme for prostate cancer.
key_points: A study of 880 men showed prostate cancer can be diagnosed through MRI scans and blood tests without an invasive biopsy.
The non-invasive method detected the disease 99 percent of the time.
Biopsies carry risks of side effects, missed cancers, and detection of harmless cancers.
The findings could reignite calls for wider targeted screening programmes for men at increased risk.

title: Deaf patient given wrong jab due to sign language error, report says
author: Beth Rose; Emma Tracey
content:
![Close-up of a person receiving an injection in the upper arm, with a healthcare worker holding a syringe and supporting the arm. The image focuses on the vaccination procedure in a clinical setting, with the background softly blurred.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a8a3/live/e8eb51e0-9b24-11f1-9a2c-6d6ac3827d20.jpg)
- Published
A deaf woman was given the wrong vaccine because she was not provided with a British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter at her doctor's surgery, a report says.
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) said disabled people were being let down by inaccessible communications.
It said the patient, Samantha, had booked a flu jab but was instead given a Covid vaccine after staff failed to show her a BSL video which would have highlighted the error. She said the experience had had a "profound impact" on her.
The Department of Health and Social Care said the "deeply upsetting stories" were "completely unacceptable" and NHS and social care organisations had a duty to make services accessible.
The PHSO investigates complaints about UK government departments, public organisations and the NHS in England.
It said public services were legally required to support people with their accessible communication needs, which might be due to a disability, neurodivergence or English not being their first language.
Samantha had booked her flu and Covid jabs for separate weeks and showed a nurse a note on her phone which said she was there for the "flu jab only", the PHSO said.
Despite that, the practice said it believed it had correctly established Samantha wanted the Covid vaccine and had got her consent through her grandmother, even though she had early-stage dementia and was not in the treatment room.
Following an investigation, the PHSO recommended the surgery should apologise and pay Samantha Â£450. It has also since signed a contract with a sign language interpreting company.
The NHS Northamptonshire Integrated Care Board said it was "very sorry" about Samantha's experience, and that it expected practices to make "reasonable adjustments to support effective communication".
The PHSO said it had found disabled people risked not getting vital information about their healthcare, finances or employment because of a lack of accessible formats such as large print or audio materials.
Since April 2020, it said it had concluded 623 investigations related to reasonable adjustments, of which 496 were upheld or partly upheld.
The report also highlighted the case of Alan Graham, who was deaf and was being treated for heart failure at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust.
When an interpreter was not available, hospital staff asked his teenage grandson to interpret for the family and tell Graham's deaf daughter that he might die.
![Alan Graham pictured holding a fish. He is wearing a khaki hat and fisherman's jacket. He has a grey beard and wears circular silver framed glasses](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/062f/live/0a9fb2e0-9b16-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Alan Graham was being treated for cancer in Birmingham when his grandson was asked to interpret serious news to the family
Following an ombudsman investigation, the trust apologised and said "we did not get things right".
They said new measures had been introduced to help deaf patients, including strengthening awareness and accessibility arrangements to ensure patients' communication needs were better met.
"We remain committed to learning from this and to providing inclusive, compassionate care for all our patients," they said.
Following the report by the ombudsman, NHS England said it was "completely unacceptable for those who are deaf or have visual loss to face barriers to accessing or understanding the healthcare they need".
It added it had recently refreshed its standards setting out how services should provide safe and effective care for those with communication needs.
The PHSO said that while it was not a regulator, it could order public organisations to pay financial compensation if it upheld a complaint.
Rebecca Hilsenrath, its chief executive, said: "When people feel they are not listened to and that their needs are not met, they lose trust in the very services designed to support them."
In its report, the PHSO highlighted North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust as a good example of providing effective communication, after it worked with local advocacy groups and deaf people to improve its service for deaf patients who reported feeling excluded.
The trust has provided guides for patients on how to access interpreting and translation services, increasing the use of interpreters by 50% in one year.
summary: A Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman report revealed that a deaf woman named Samantha was given the wrong vaccine after being denied a British Sign Language interpreter at her surgery. The report highlighted multiple cases where disabled patients faced inaccessible communications, including a hospital asking a teenager to interpret his grandfather's critical medical news. The ombudsman recommended apologies and compensation in the investigated cases, prompting calls from health authorities for better accessibility and reasonable adjustments.
key_points: A deaf patient booked a flu jab but received a Covid vaccine instead due to a lack of a BSL interpreter.
The PHSO report found disabled people are frequently let down by inaccessible communications in public services.
In another highlighted case, a deaf patient's teenage grandson was asked to interpret critical end-of-life information.
The surgery involved in Samantha's case was recommended to apologize and pay £450, and has since hired a sign language interpreting company.
NHS England stated that communication barriers are unacceptable and noted that standards for accessible care have been refreshed.

title: Shropshire farmers scared about shortage in bluetongue vaccine
author: Charlie Stubbs
content:
![There is a man in a dark green polo shirt, with 'NFU' in yellow letters next to it. He has grey thin hair and is standing. To his left, there is his buggy, which is gret and has a window. To his right, there are cows.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/3803/live/1e89b160-9b08-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Richard Yates originally only vaccinated his cows against bluetongue but when cases were reported nationally, he also did his sheep
- Published
A farmer in Shropshire says he is worried for animals across the country because of the spread of an outbreak of the potentially fatal bluetongue virus amid a vaccine shortage.
Richard Yates, from Middleton Scriven near Bridgnorth, at first only vaccinated his cattle, but once cases started to rise in the South West, he jabbed his sheep.
It is now "extremely difficult to get the vaccine", he said and warned farmers could be faced with "considerable losses" if their animals died from the outbreak,.
The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was "working closely with the industry and is putting processes in for additional vaccine supplies".
Bluetongue is an insect-borne viral disease affecting sheep and cattle among other animals, mainly spread by biting midges, which thrive in long, hot summers like the one the UK is experiencing.
There are currently 456 cases in the UK, external, none in Shropshire, but that number is expected to rise across the country.
The UK's chief veterinary officer committed earlier this month to "ramp up" testing and wanted all farmers to get the vaccine when it became available.
![There is a herd of sheep in a field of brown grass and waste. There is around 50 and they have white and black heads and wool coats the same colour as the grass.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1539/live/23f41b40-9b08-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Yates got his sheep vaccinated before the vaccine shortage
Yates said the virus was a big issue in Belgium and the Netherlands two years ago and killed cattle and sheep there "in their droves".
"[Animals] can be healthy one day and dead the next," he added.
"It can also cause abortions, stillbirths, reducing fertility. It is devastating."
Yates said the vaccinations he gave his animals last year could still give them some protection.
"There will be some benefit if the animals are vaccinated last year [as it is] kicking around in their system," he said.
"But it evolves and mutates. Twenty-five years ago, there was a different strain of bluetongue.
"I remember going to the old Royal Show and that was the next big problem that was coming our way. We all vaccinated and after a year it disappeared."
'Worst outbreak'
Vets across the county have encouraged farmers to take up the vaccine by going on to a waiting list.
The shortage was because of issues with supply and demand because of "unprecedented levels" of need, according to Susan Carr, a farm vet at Severn Edge Practice in Bridgnorth.
"There is about 20,000 doses on our waiting list but I can imagine other practices are going through the same," she added.
"We are importing a lot of stock at the minute from Europe; it is a UK-licensed vaccine but there just isn't the stock in Europe.
"It's just taking time and obviously at the minute that's not what people want to hear."
Carr has worked as a vet for 12 years and said, about this outbreak, she had never seen it so bad.
"This is the worst notifiable disease outbreak I have had to deal with," she added.
"The only other [outbreak] we have had was bird flu a few years back."
"[It was] pretty bad around here and some of us did go and work alongside the ministry there with outbreaks but this has by far been sadly the the most the biggest one I've seen."
The spokesperson for Defra said they recognised how concerning bluetongue was for farmers and urged them and vets to place vaccine orders.
"There is a wide range of support available to help farmers protect their livestock and we will continue to monitor the situation closely," they added.
summary: Shropshire farmers and veterinarians are expressing deep concern over a vaccine shortage as the insect-borne bluetongue virus spreads across the UK, threatening livestock with death and reduced fertility. Farmer Richard Yates warned that animals could face considerable losses, while local vets report unprecedented demand with thousands of doses currently on waiting lists. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) stated it is working closely with the industry to secure additional vaccine supplies.
key_points: A shortage of the bluetongue vaccine has made it extremely difficult for farmers to protect their sheep and cattle.
There are currently 456 cases of the potentially fatal, insect-borne virus in the UK, with numbers expected to rise.
Local vets report unprecedented demand, with a single practice in Bridgnorth holding a waiting list for about 20,000 doses.
Defra stated it is working with the industry and putting processes in place for additional vaccine supplies.

title: Bowel cancer cases in under-50s at record high in Scotland
author: Aimee Stanton; Susie Forrest
content:
![Anona Gauld is wearing a pink and black spotty shirt and black glasses. She is smiling and there is a 40th birthday cake in front of her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/0751/live/be585630-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld had just turned 40 when she was diagnosed with cancer
- Published
The number of people under the age of 50 being diagnosed with bowel cancer in Scotland has reached a record high, with almost 290 new cases in 2024, new figures show.
Bowel cancer is the fourth most common cancer in Scotland and is more often diagnosed in older people, with those over 50 offered screening in an attempt to detect it early.
However, new figures from Public Health Scotland, external show incidence has jumped by 38% in the under-50s over the past decade, with rates among younger women increasing by 56% in comparison with 24% in younger men.
Last month, the Scottish government asked the UK National screening committee to look at lowering the age for bowel screening to 45, to target younger patients.
Anona Gauld is one of a growing number of women under 50 being diagnosed with colorectal cancer, the medical name for bowel cancers.
She told the BBC her journey towards diagnosis started when she turned 40 in March 2023 and couldn't manage a birthday glass of fizz.
She'd had a mysterious pain in her shoulder for several weeks, which got worse every time she drank alcohol.
Gauld, from Stonehaven, thought she'd pulled a muscle or had been lying awkwardly in bed but by August she had been diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer, which had spread to her liver.
![Anona Gauld is wearing a white shirt and black glasses. She has mid length brown hair and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/422a/live/d22e2810-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer
She had been going back and forth to her GP over several months but believes cancer wasn't initially considered, partly because of her age.
"One doctor even told me it was because my bra was too tight," she said.
"It was just a mystery."
Doctors later said the pain in her shoulder was actually coming from her liver, where they discovered a 13cm (5in) secondary tumour which had spread from her bowel.
![Lathan is sat in the driver's seat of the car and is smiling at the cancer. Anona is sat next to him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8857/live/cce81140-9af2-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Anona has three children aged between 15 and 21
"It was a big shock," Gauld says.
"I was young, I was healthy. I had a healthy diet and you don't think it's going to happen to you."
She had chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and then surgery on her liver and bowel in 2024.
Last year the cancer came back in her liver, and since then she's been back on treatment.
"People can have stage 4 cancer and live for many years," she says.
"It is scary, because I've never asked my oncologist for any timeline or anything like that, because I don't want to know.
"I think it's just a case of living your life."
What is causing the rise in bowel cancer?
PHS said no definitive cause had been identified for the increase in bowel cancer in people aged under 50 and different potential causes were being investigated.
However, research suggests six in 10 colorectal cancers might be prevented, external through reducing weight, lowering consumption of red and processed meat, increasing dietary fibre and cutting down on alcohol.
Richard Wilson, professor of gastro-intestinal oncology at the University of Glasgow, told BBC Scotland the causes among the under-50s may be different compared with older patients, because of new risk factors that emerged after the 1990s.
"Ultra processed foods, we think, are the huge driver, because their use across all age groups has really increased," he said.
Wilson added that exposure to pesticides as well as micro and nanoplastics might also be factors.
"These tiny broken-down bits of plastic are in the air, in the water, in our food, and we're really concerned about that," he said.
"And then forever chemicals from non-stick frying pans, all of these affect the microbiome in the gut. That's the common denominator.
"We think all these things disrupt the healthy microbiome, cause inflammation, and might predispose to cancer."
Every year thousands of people across Scotland are diagnosed with bowel cancer.
In 2024, 4,275 cases were recorded - slightly down on 2023's figure of 4,395.
NHS inform, external lists the following as potential symptoms of bowel cancer:
- blood in your poo (stools)
- bleeding from your bottom
- a recent change in your poo, particularly looser poo or pooing more regularly
- new pain in your abdomen (tummy) that won't go away
- you've recently lost weight without trying
- more pale and tired than usual
Bowel screening is currently offered to people in Scotland, external aged 50 to 74 years old every two years - this is the same for people in England, external and Wales, external. In Northern Ireland, external screening is offered to people aged 60 to 74 every two years.
A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: "The Scottish government recognises that bowel cancers are occurring at higher rates that previously in people under the age of 50 and have submitted a proposal to the UK National screening committee review bowel screening eligibility to consider offering this to younger age groups."
However, Bowel Cancer UK chief executive Genevieve Edwards said any changes to Scotland's screening programme must be based on "robust evidence" and be supported by the NHS having the capacity to deliver them safely and effectively.
She said the rise in cases among people under 50 showed the need for further research and greater awareness.
"Scotland's focus must stay on diagnosing bowel cancer earlier and ensuring that everyone receives the right care at the right time," Edwards said.
Trends in other cancers
Bowel remains one of the most common cancer types in Scotland, alongside prostate, breast and lung - these cancers account for more than half (55%) of all diagnoses.
In men, a record number of men were diagnosed with prostate cancer in Scotland in 2024, the same year Sir Chris Hoy revealed he was being treated for the disease, with the number of diagnoses increasing by 6% compared to the year before.
Malignant melanoma of the skin (skin cancer) has also increased in men, rising by 28%.
However, there were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, oesophageal cancer and cancer of unknown primary in men.
In women, there were also significant increases in the rates of breast cancer (8%), colorectal cancer (8%), and malignant melanoma of the skin (by more than a third, 37%).
There were no cases of cervical cancer in women under 25 following the introduction of the HPV vaccine.
There were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, cancer of unknown primary, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and kidney cancer.
